It delegates now, because `openCategory` has carried the right mapping all along.
- v9.64 — **Nothing in the Featured row wears a filter's name any more (queue 318).** His words: *"Also in the effects menu filters are showing up in the featured menu"*. Strictly they were not filters — `tealorange`, `faded`, `bleachbypass` and `crossprocess` are single colour EFFECTS — but each is ALSO the id of a ready-made filter built from that same effect and leading with the same name, so the carousel showed four tiles called Teal & Orange, Faded Film, Bleach Bypass and Cross Process on the tab whose entire job is to not be the Filters tab. From the outside that is filters in the featured row, and he is right that it is wrong. They are replaced with visual effects that have no filter twin, and all four remain one search or one category away and still live inside the filters that use them. **Cleaning the list fixes today; the browser now also refuses any featured id that names a filter, and that is what stops it returning** — the list is the kind that gets appended to and the collision lives in a different file, so it is invisible unless someone happens to read both at once. The test plants a real filter id into the featured list and checks no tile appears for it. It also checks every featured id resolves to a real effect, because the builder drops unknown ids silently: a swap with a typo in it would not throw, it would just leave the carousel shorter and look fine.
- v9.65 — **Noise gets a Square/Round grain toggle, and its preview grain is half the size (queue 319).** His words: *"For the noise preview make the noise smaller so it doesn't look shit, and also give the noise effect a toggle to circle noise or square noise"*. **Round punches each grain cell down to the disc inscribed in it**, so the corners of the grid take no noise at all — specks scattered over the frame instead of a solid tiling. Measured: 80% of the pixels square grain touches, against the pi/4 = 79% a circle in a square has to give. Square stays the default, because it is what the effect has always done and changing what an existing project renders as is not the same as adding a control. It is skipped entirely at grain size 1, where the cell is one pixel and the circle inscribed in it is that pixel — the arithmetic would cost work on the default settings to produce no difference. **The preview was set to grain size 4, and the rule that says it should not be is written three paragraphs above it in the same file, about dither:** two plate-pixels is what survives being scaled up and back down, and past that "the cell stops reading as error diffusion and starts reading as mosaic, and a thumbnail that overstates the effect is the same failure as one that understates it". Noise was set to 4 in the same pass that reasoned dither down to 2, and nobody applied the second half of that sentence to it — so the tile advertised Noise as chunky mosaic while the effect's own default is fine speckle. It is 2 now. Amount and colour are untouched: the complaint was the size of the grain, not its loudness.
- v9.66 — **Lightning reworked: forks, taper, and a bright core inside a glow (queue 320).** His words: *"The lightning effect looks pretty bad, give it a work over"*. **What was there was fourteen straight segments displaced by two sine waves, drawn at ONE width with ONE falloff** — and three things follow from that, all three of which are why it read as a zigzag line rather than as lightning: a sine is smooth, so the "jaggedness" undulated and repeated instead of breaking; one width top to bottom, so nothing tapered and nothing died out; one narrow falloff, so there was no bright core inside a wider glow, which is the thing that makes a bolt look like it is emitting light rather than being a stroke someone drew. Now it is a hashed random-walk channel with two to four forks that leave it, thin out and stop, a taper along every path, and two passes — a wide dim halo in the layer's colour, then a narrow near-white core over it, because a real channel is blown out and the tint lives in the glow around it. **Hashed rather than random, deliberately:** this runs in the exporter as well as the preview, and `Math.random` would make an export flicker differently from what was previewed, which is unfixable from the outside — the test renders the same frame twice and compares. The other three assertions are the three absences, each of which the old implementation failed by construction: a single bolt now puts more than one strand across some rows (forks), is measurably wider near the top than the bottom (taper), and has a peak brightness well above its own mean (core inside glow). Bolts, Intensity and Colour are untouched, so an existing project keeps its settings and just looks better.
- v9.67 — **Mask and Motion Blur (Object) select like every other tile instead of committing on tap — queue 321 (partial), clause 1.** His words: *"With the mask effect when you press on it it instantly adds instead of previewing"*. The queue-277 rework made every ordinary tile select-then-Add; these two are PSEUDO tiles — they change the LAYER rather than adding an effect instance — and the multi-select was built around instances, so both were left calling their action straight from the click. **From the outside that distinction does not exist:** one tile in the grid behaved unlike all the others and shut the browser on you. They badge and wait for Add now. Both actions gained a quiet mode, for the same reason `addEffect` grew one in that rework — a batch runs several and closes once at the end, so an entry that closed the browser itself would tear it down under the second item in its own list — and the mask EDITOR only opens on the single-tap path, since in a batch it would land on top of whatever else was picked. The commit path is routed by the same table the tiles are built from, so a third pseudo entry cannot be added to the grid and left out of Add. **What these two still cannot do is preview themselves, and that is not a gap:** a mask has no result to show until you have drawn one, which is what the editor that opens on Add is for. **Clause 2 — the on-screen trackpad while editing a mask — is not in this release** and the entry stays open for it; the pad is currently bespoke to the drawing bar, so doing it properly means extracting it rather than writing a second one.
- v9.68 — **Editing a mask gets the same precision pad the drawing tool has, and it is now one control rather than two — queue 321 complete.** His words: *"make it when editing the mask and where it actually masks, you can use the touch pad thing like when editing points on a shape"*. **The gain is the whole reason the control exists:** it runs at project-width / 640, which is finer than touching the canvas — on a phone a finger pixel on the canvas is about 3.5 project px and on the pad about 1.7 — so a mask point can be put somewhere a fingertip physically cannot reach. **It is extracted rather than copied**, and that is not tidiness: this project's standing note about the timeline glide and the sliders is exactly this situation, where two surfaces meant to feel identical each got their own copy and one was retuned without the other; the number above is precisely the kind of thing that gets retuned in one place. The pad appears only when a point is selected, because that is what it moves and a pad that silently did nothing would be worse than none. Nudging goes through the same write path a drag does, so it keyframes, undoes and saves identically. The test asserts the SENSITIVITY, not just that the point moved — a pad running one-for-one with the finger would look right, work, and be pointless. Two fixture traps on the way: the suite's project is 64x48, so the gain reduces a 64px swipe to six pixels AND the write clamps to the project box, which had the first run reporting the corner of a tiny canvas as if it were a measurement.
- v9.69 — **The eraser rubs out part of a stroke instead of deleting the whole drawing — queue 322 (partial), clause 4.** His words: *"erase should work like an eraser not just delete the whole drawing"*. It found the stroke nearest the finger and spliced the entire subpath out, so touching the tail of a long line took the line. Now it removes the points inside its reach and each surviving run becomes its own subpath — rub through the middle of a stroke and you get two, which is what an eraser does. The layer format was already multi-subpath, so nothing downstream needed teaching. **Two things worth recording.** Subpaths the eraser did not touch are kept BY REFERENCE rather than rebuilt: undo here is snapshots of the subpath list, taken as a shallow copy on the stated grounds that strokes are never mutated in place, so handing back fresh arrays for untouched strokes would still be correct while quietly making every snapshot a deep copy of the whole drawing. And there is a case the obvious version misses — the hit test measures to the SEGMENT, so a finger over the middle of a long straight span is "on" the stroke while being far from every point of it; falling through to the old behaviour there would delete the whole line, which is the bug, so that path splits the nearest segment instead. The test drops a 81-point stroke and rubs its middle, then checks both ends survived and that a real gap opened — a version that shortened the stroke from one end would pass a naive "it still exists" check.
- v9.70 — **Draw-on: a drawing can be trimmed by Draw from / Draw to, both keyframable, so it draws itself on live — queue 322 (partial), clause 2.** His words: *"it has an option to change the start and end point, so you could do a cool effect with key frames to make it look like it's being drawn live"*. Keyframe **Draw to** from 0 to 100 and the line appears as if being drawn. **Measured across the WHOLE drawing, not per stroke.** A sketch is several strokes, and trimming each to the same fraction would draw all of them on at once — every stroke growing together, which is not what being drawn looks like. One cumulative length over every stroke in order means Draw to sweeps through the first, then the second, the way a hand would. **By length, not by point index**, and that is the difference a naive version would fail invisibly: points are not evenly spaced, because the sampler drops one every 2.5 device px along the FINGER's path, so a fast flick spreads them further apart in project space than a slow curve — an index-based trim would draw the line on at a speed that depended on how fast it was drawn. The test cuts inside a two-point stroke, which an index-based trim cannot land in at all. Curve flags survive on interior points so a trimmed stroke is as smooth as an untrimmed one, and the two cut ends are marked hard, because an interpolated point is not one he placed and rounding through it would bend the line somewhere he never drew. Closed paths are left alone — trimming one turns a filled shape into a filled crescent, which is not what "start and end point" describes. **Clause 3 (re-entering drawing mode on an existing drawing) is the last one open on this item.**
- v9.71 — **A drawing can be re-opened and drawn on — queue 322 complete.** His words: *"there should be a button to re edit the drawing so you can draw more or erase"*. Edit Points on a sketch now carries **✎ Draw more**, which re-opens the sketching tool ON that drawing: new strokes join it, and the eraser can reach what is already there, which is the "or erase" half. **The failure this had to avoid is a second layer.** A session that starts empty and then commits a stroke BUILDS a drawing — that is what the first stroke of any session does — so re-opening the tool without adopting the existing one leaves two sketches stacked on the canvas, looking almost right and impossible to edit as one thing. The session is adopted instead: layer id, strokes, colour and brush width all seeded from the layer, so the commit re-fits it rather than creating a sibling. Counting layers is what the test asserts, not "did a stroke get added". The strokes come back through `evalShapeSubs` rather than straight off the layer, because they are stored normalised to the layer's box, may be keyframed, and a single-stroke drawing keeps them in `points` rather than `subs` — three ways to get this wrong that one function already knows about. **A note on how this nearly went wrong:** the first attempt anchored the insertion on a line of code that appears twice, and landed the whole block inside `stop()` — which also swallowed that function's closing brace and the start of the next one. The syntax check passed, because the braces happened to balance. Reverted and re-done by line position; the suite is what caught it.
- v9.72 — **The three audio sliders explain themselves — queue 325 (partial).** His words: *"I'm confused by the three audio sliders so explain better"*. The entry did not know which three; they are Audio React's **Sensitivity / Smoothing / Threshold**, the only set of exactly three audio sliders in the app, and each was a bare word over a track with no explanation anywhere on the sheet — three pieces of jargon and no way in. Each now carries a line under its label saying what it does TO THE PICTURE, not to the signal ("attack and release envelope" is true and useless), and naming the symptom you would be trying to fix when you reach for it, because that is how anyone actually finds the right slider. Under the label rather than beside it: the value readout already owns the right-hand end of that row, and a description squeezed between them is the one nobody reads. The test checks all three, and that none of them is explained by repeating its own name — "Smoothing: how much smoothing" is the failure mode of every hurried hint and it reads as an explanation right up until you need one. **Also closed off the other half of that entry:** the Presets card was already given live per-layer previews in v9.29, which is exactly what he asked for there, so that clause needed confirming rather than building.
- v9.73 — **Squish in a corner: measured, and now guarded — queue 323 (partial), its first clause.** His words: *"For the squish effect make it so it actually works in corners"*. **It already does, and here are the numbers rather than an assurance.** A 160px ball hung 40px past each wall it touches, in a 400x400 comp, counting lit pixels along the frame edges: against the right wall alone 138 → 51; against the bottom alone 138 → 54; **in the bottom-right corner 109 → 16 across and 109 → 18 down** — both axes bind, and the corner squashes harder than either wall on its own. So this clause needed a test rather than a fix, and it has one now, because a claim of "works fine" with nothing behind it is worth very little against a report that says otherwise. **The test uses a CIRCLE and that is load-bearing:** squashed against a wall a circle lands tangent and its coverage of that frame edge drops, while a square flattens and covers MORE — measuring a square read as "the fix made it worse" earlier in this same investigation and cost a wrong conclusion. Each wall is also measured on its own first, so a corner failure cannot hide behind a wall that was not working either. **The other clause — reacting to effect-driven movement — is still open**, and is the ~20-site plate migration written up in the entry.
- v9.74 — **Squish reacts to a layer moved by an EFFECT — queue 323 complete.** His words: *"if you have a shake effect or any effect that makes the object move, the squish should apply, currently if a shake makes it move the squish doesn't do anything"*. **THREE things had to be right, and each one ALONE changed nothing** — which is a good way to conclude the wrong thing twice, and did, across two earlier sittings that ended in a revert. (1) **Every effect plate was comp-sized.** Squish deliberately renders the layer into a plate PADDED past every wall, because the overhang is the part it squashes back in — and each of the layer's other effects allocated a comp-sized plate INSIDE that padded one and clipped the overhang away before Squish could measure it. Plates now inherit the TARGET's extent and origin: **43 call sites across 17 render paths**, done per-function rather than by find-and-replace, because they do not share one convention — most work in plate pixels, `drawPixelate` works in project units, the mask passes differ again. Verified byte-identical first, with the order untouched, which is the property that made it safe to put in front of every effect in the app. (2) **Squish was pinned to composite INNERMOST**, so it measured the layer before the shake had moved it — mid-frame, no penetration, correctly doing nothing — and the shake then pushed it over a wall nobody was enforcing. The pin is inverted; the note explaining the old direction is kept, because its reasoning was right for the code as it stood. (3) **The box deciding whether a wall is worth looking at is built from the transform matrix**, which knows nothing about an effect displacing pixels at render time, so the pass early-outed before either of the other two fixes could help. It now allows the layer's own half-extent — **for named movers only**: the first version padded for ANY effect and broke `[squish, bulge]`, because a bulge does not move the layer, it redistributes it, and a much larger plate changed the geometry it warps. **The test uses a CIRCLE**, which is load-bearing: squashed against a wall a ball lands tangent and its coverage of that frame edge drops, while a square flattens and covers MORE — measuring a square read as "the fix made it worse" earlier in this investigation and cost a wrong conclusion.
- v9.75 — **The two preset save buttons now say what each one keeps (queue 329).** His words: *"In the presets presets menu what is the difference between pressing save this layer as preset and save current effects? If none then just make one button not two"*. **There is a difference, so the merge he offered is not the right answer** — one saves the whole layer including its transform and animation, the other saves the effect stack and nothing else — but that he could not tell which was which from the buttons IS the defect, and so were the headings above them: "My presets" and "Effect looks" were as interchangeable as the buttons. They read **Save look + animations…** and **Save effects only…** now, under **Look + animations** and **Effects only**. "Look + animations" is not a new phrase: it is exactly what the saved rows already call themselves a few lines up, so the words describing the thing are the words on the button that makes it. Neither label needs a sentence under it, which is what he has asked twice to stop doing — the contrast between them carries it. **The test asserts the DISTINCTION rather than the wording**: that the two do not read the same, that one names the animation and the other names effects only, and that the section headings differ. Pinning exact strings would fail the next time either is nudged while saying nothing about whether they can be told apart — and the old pair passed a naive "they differ" check while telling you nothing, which is how the question came to be asked.
- v9.76 — the Filters tab shows photographs again, and each look now demonstrates on a picture chosen for it (his cars included) instead of the same sunset sixteen times. Three separate faults: the re-mount that repaints tiles once the JPEGs decode was finding them by the effects browser's CSS class, so the inspector's filter tiles were never swept and kept the drawn stand-in all session; the preload list was a hand-kept array that had fallen four names behind the tables and was missing every car; and a picture painted before its photo arrived was cached rather than discarded. The sweep now reads a registry of mounted canvases, the preload set is derived from the tables, and a provisional paint is never kept. Queue 359 (the new car-photo filters themselves remain open as #349).
- v9.77 — saving a preset now shows up in the Presets card straight away, instead of only after you close the card and reopen it. Four things change the two preset lists — two save buttons and two ✕ — and each had to remember to rebuild the panel; three did, and the fourth ("Save look + animations…") runs through a function in app.js that knows nothing about the inspector, so the one path that could not see the panel was the one that left it stale. Rather than add the call there and leave the same trap set, the rule moved to the single point every change to either list passes through — the write itself — and the three now-redundant hand-written refreshes came out. Queue 330.
- v9.78 — the Presets card, tidied: the explanation block at the top is gone, each **Save…** button now leads its own section instead of sitting under the list (so the thing you opened the card to do is not below the fold on a phone), and the ✕ on every preset row is a drawn cross rather than the character — the third time that same defect has been reported, and the same fix as the × in queue 209 and the + in 296: a font decides where its ink sits, geometry does not. Three of the nine clauses in #331 (partial); search, rename and tags are the rest of that entry and are not done. **Correction to v9.78's predecessor:** v9.77 said three redundant refreshes came out and only two did — the third replacement silently matched nothing because I asserted the other two and not that one. It is out now, and that is the argument for asserting every edit, not most of them.
- v9.79 — the Presets card can be searched and organised: a search box and a row of tag chips at the top, hold a preset to rename or tag it, a tag becomes a group you can filter by, and untagged presets sink to the bottom. Tags live in a sidecar map keyed by name, because both preset stores are keyed by name — which makes a rename a re-key, so renaming onto a name already in use is refused rather than resolved (it would merge two saved looks and lose one, silently), and the tags move with the name instead of being orphaned. This entry had been parked on "do it after queue 37 unifies the stores"; #37 shipped as the preset PREVIEW screen and never touched them, so that was waiting on nothing. Closes queue 331.
- v9.80 — the shake section is his own cars, and it is called **Shakes / Movement** now. All four photos he sent are in use across the seven effects rather than one repeated, arranged so no two neighbouring tiles share a car — a category whose tiles are all the same picture tells you nothing about which effect is which, which is the fault the Filters tab had. No new machinery was needed: that category already used the inset CARD form, which is what makes a shake visible at all (a full-frame subject that shakes just swings its own edges through the tile). Queue 332.
- v9.81 — **Done adds the effects you picked**, instead of throwing them away. It called close() and nothing else, so a numbered selection of eight vanished when you pressed the button that says you are finished — which is the whole of "all the effects I have selected do nothing", and the same defect reported again from the other side as "it's just there to fuck you over". That was a design mistake of mine: the button predates the multi-select and was never revisited when picking arrived. And the sweep he asked for is now a TEST rather than a one-off pass — it opens all twelve categories, taps all 198 tiles including Mask and Motion Blur (Object), and fails if any one of them applies itself instead of selecting, or fails to reach the live preview. Every tile currently behaves. Queue 333.
- v9.82 — the cars come off the filter tiles. They were sent for the shake section — "All just for the shake section" — and I had spread them across five filters that never asked for one. Teal & Orange is the bay, Bleach Bypass the beach run, Cross Process the estuary at dusk, VHS the skyline, and Comic Ink the dog — which reads far better as line art than a cityscape did anyway, since the answer there was never "a car", it was "something that outlines". A test now fails if any filter demonstrates on a car, so when the tuff filters arrive the cars land there on purpose rather than by drift. Queue 371; the shake section (#332) is unchanged and still uses all four.
- v9.83 — **Motion Blur (Object) is a real effect now.** It was a flag on the layer, not a stack entry, which is exactly why it could never go inside a Filter — a Filter is a container of effects. It is an ordinary row today: reorderable, keyframable, swipe-to-delete, and it goes in a Filter. Projects saved with the old flag convert on load, and the effect is inserted INNERMOST because that is where the old one always composited — appending it would have quietly re-ordered the render on every project that had both an effect and the blur. Proven rather than asserted: a fingerprint of the render was captured BEFORE any edit, and the legacy flag, a migrated project and a hand-written effect all reproduce it exactly at five times. Cameras are untouched — `cam.motionBlur` is a different feature with its own renderer, and a camera cannot hold an effect at all, so a migration that treated all layers alike would have silently killed camera blur. Queue 335.
- v9.84 — three things. **Trimming a clip now needs a HOLD on touch** (about half a second) before the grip will drag, and the grip turns the signature colour to say it is live — brushing a 13px target while scrolling used to retime the clip with nothing to distinguish a grab from a graze. A mouse still trims instantly, because a mouse-down on that target cannot happen by accident. **Effect panels no longer carry an explanation paragraph** — the fourth time that has been asked for, so it is now a rule rather than an instance: the panel stopped rendering descriptions rather than 190 of them being deleted, so the text survives as the browser tooltip and as the reference for tutorials. **And motion blur cranks four times harder** — the shutter was clamped to a single frame of travel, which is what a real shutter does and exactly why the strongest setting looked timid. Queue 336, 378, 379.
- v9.85 — holding the timeline no longer offers to add a benchmark. Only the ADD is gone: renaming, removing and clearing a marker still live on that same long-press, because they act on a marker you are already pointing at and dropping the whole gesture would have taken them with it. Adding one still works two other ways (the timecode chip, and M on a keyboard), checked before this route was removed. An empty stretch of ruler now opens nothing at all rather than an empty menu. Queue 337.
- v9.86 — the phone's Move-clip and Extend-edge buttons are no longer the same drawing. They differed only in whether one box was closed or open at one end — about four pixels of ink, on two buttons sitting side by side. The desktop pair had this exact complaint fixed at queue 235 and the phone copy was left behind, so that answer is copied rather than a third pair invented: MOVE is a solid block with a double chevron (the clip picks up and travels), EXTEND is an outlined block open at the near edge with a dashed span (that edge stretches, and the dashes are the new material). The test asserts fill-versus-outline rather than the path data, so it still means something after the next nudge. Queue 338.
- v9.87 — every layer-category card now has its own gradient ring, in the colours of its own icon, with a shine that sweeps around it and a glow that breathes — and no two cards are in step. The backgrounds are untouched, as asked: the change is the line, not the fill. The palettes are LIFTED from each icon's gradient stops rather than matched by eye, so they cannot drift apart when an icon is retouched — except Speed, which is deliberately red-dominant because taking its dial's real colours put it next to Presets and the two rings read the same. Each card gets its own duration AND a negative delay, so they start at different points of the cycle rather than separating later. Queue 339.
- v9.88 — the card rings now trace the button edge instead of hovering a pixel inside it, and the glow is a fraction of what it was. Both were his, on the release an hour old. The inset one is worth knowing: the cards keep a 1px transparent border for layout, so a ring at `inset: 0` draws against the PADDING box — one pixel in from the outline you can actually see, which at 3x reads exactly as "slightly inside it". The glow had been judged on a 380px screenshot, where a soft halo looks like a bit of glow and on a real phone is a headlight. Queue 339 follow-up.
- v9.89 — making a new element no longer dumps a project into your Projects list. It still creates a workspace — an element is saved FROM layers, so something has to hold them while you draw — but that workspace is a DRAFT now: hidden from Projects, shown at the top of the Elements tab with a dashed card that says what to do with it, and it opens straight back to where you were building. Queue 340 clause 1; the look of the add-element menu (clause 2) is not done.
- v9.90 — the home film grain is now deliberately STILL on phones and still moving on PC, which is what he asked for. It was already still on his phone and nothing in the stylesheet was doing that — the device was dropping the animation on its own — so the look he liked was an accident that a future iOS release could have taken away. It is a rule now, at the same 700px breakpoint the rest of the file uses, and it makes the phone marginally cheaper to run. Queue 341.
- v9.91 — tapping an element on the Elements tab now OPENS it to edit, instead of shoving it into whichever project happened to be open. The question that had been left hanging — is an element a clip you drop in, or a small project you build and re-use — is answered by where you are standing: on Home there is often no project open at all, and that tap used to reply "Open a project first", which is a tap that does nothing wearing an error message. Inserting already has a home that always makes sense (Add → Elements, inside a project), and it is still on the card's ⋯ menu. Editing opens a transparent draft and reuses the insert path wholesale, so both routes are the same code aimed at different projects. Queue 342 clause 1.
- v9.92 — the film grain moves again, on the phone as well as PC, and it stops the moment a project is open. He reversed v9.90 and both halves of that mattered. Deleting the phone rule alone would have changed nothing: the grain was never animating on his phone even before that rule existed — iOS was dropping it, because animating background-position repaints the whole screen every step, which is exactly the work a phone browser sheds. The offsets are transforms now, which run on the compositor. And his own condition turned out to be the better design: the home screen stays in the DOM behind the editor, so an unpaused field was boiling underneath every rendered frame for something nobody can see. Queue 341.
- v9.93 — three at once. **The anchor can go anywhere** — it was clamped to 0-100% of the layer's own box, so a pivot could never sit outside the thing being pivoted (a door hinging off its frame, an arm swinging from a shoulder); the renderer never clamped it, so this was purely the two controls. **Three explanation paragraphs are gone** from Move & Transform — the Z/parallax note in both places it appeared, and the behaviours pair. **And Custom elements has a multi-coloured ring** in its own icon's four colours, using the same masked ring built for the layer cards rather than a second technique that would drift away from it. Queue 344, 345, 346.
- v9.94 — two stacking bugs, same shape: something unimportant painting over something you were trying to use. The **benchmark line no longer runs through the layer-preview column** — the pin hangs from the ruler row, and it was the ROW's z-index fighting the sticky heads, not the pin's, which is why lowering the marker would have done nothing. And the **loading pill now sits behind the panels** instead of over them; lowered rather than hidden, because a loading state you cannot see at all is worse than one partly covered — it is the only thing saying the app has not frozen. Queue 348, 393.
- v9.95 — **THE BLACK BAR, FOUND (#187).** Seven rounds have chased this since v5.49 and each one fixed a real but different thing: the missing `viewport-fit=cover`, the `#000` document canvas (v6.85), the canvas that had the colour but none of the light (v7.02), the slam's flat ring (v7.87), the overscan that broke PC (v8.54). **It was `#home-screen::after`** — the second of home's two drifting light layers — sitting at `inset: 0` while carrying `hm-drift`, which translates it up to 8% of its own box and scales it 1 → 1.12. At the `to` frame that puts its left edge at 2% of the screen: **measured at 380x820, a 7px strip down the LEFT edge with a hard seam at x=7, 44% darker than the pixels beside it** (luminance 13.4 against 19.3). His two reports fall out of that one number and no other theory explained both. It **CREEPS** because the miss is at one end of a 12s ease-in-out `alternate`, so it opens and closes over six seconds rather than appearing. It **MOVED EDGES** because the other end of the same cycle (translate −6%, scale 1) uncovers the RIGHT instead — and the reason you only ever see the left one is that the pool is centred at 30% x, so losing it beside the light is a 44% drop while losing it at the far edge, past `transparent 60%`, is worth nothing. **Why six rounds of measurement could not see it: a pseudo-element is not in the DOM.** `querySelectorAll` cannot return it and it has no `getBoundingClientRect`, so every previous investigation walked the elements, compared rects against the viewport, correctly reported that nothing falls short — and was structurally incapable of finding the thing that did. Two whole families of theory were disproven on the way and are written into the entry so nobody re-derives them: no screen-sized element leaves a gap on any edge (home, editor, both transitions), and nothing uncovers the ground even mid-slam — proven by repainting the document canvas magenta and screenshotting, 0 marker pixels at 380x820 and 1440x900. **The fix is the same one its sibling got in v8.54: overhang the box so the drift cannot walk it off the screen.** `-12%` is arithmetic, not taste — the binding frame is `from`, where the right edge sits at `f − .06(1 + 2f)` short, so `f` must clear .068 for the layer to reach the edge at all; .12 leaves ~17px of margin at 380 and holds on all four edges at every frame. The gradient's position is compensated — `(.30 + .12)/1.24` and `(.78 + .12)/1.24` — so the pool lands exactly where it did and the look does not move (measured: mean luminance change across the middle of the screen 0.8 of ~19, i.e. under 5%, and all of it is light now reaching the edges). **The durable part is the test**, and it is shaped by the failure: it reconstructs each pseudo-element's box arithmetically from computed style, and it STEPS the animation across 21 samples end to end, because the offending frame is at one end of the cycle and a single reading lands there about never. Three control assertions stop it going quietly green — home must still be a full-viewport surface, both pseudo animations must be found, and at least four samples must have a non-identity transform. Mutation-checked by putting `inset: 0` back: caught, 30.4px uncovered.
- v9.96 — **The Elements browser is worth opening now (queue 340 complete).** His words: *"when you press the add element button the menu is not thought and looks lazy and shit, make it good"*. One 380px screenshot held every fault. **The search field stopped half way across the phone** — `.fxb-search-input` is styled for a flex COLUMN parent, and the effect browser appends it straight into the root where `align-items: stretch` gives it the width, while this browser wrapped it in an unstyled div and an `<input>`'s intrinsic ~20-character width won: **176px of a 380px screen**, hard against the left margin. **The tiles inherited the effect browser's four fixed columns** — right for a glyph, wrong for a photograph of a whole composition, which got 78px each on a phone; `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(108px, 1fr))` is 3 across a phone and 5 in the 680px desktop panel and needs no breakpoint to say so. **Every element without a thumbnail was the same blue gradient**, so a screenful was one colour repeated; they walk a six-gradient ring by index now — deliberately not a hash of the name, which is the decision `addmenu.js` already made and wrote down for the tab palettes (a hash gives every tile a hue and no two of them any relationship, which reads as accidental). **And the empty state was one line of italic grey text at the top of a black screen — pointing at a door that is not there.** It read *"select some layers, then Elements ▸ Save selection as element"*, and that item was removed from the Add menu (addmenu.js:216 says why: it acts on a selection, and that menu only ever opens when nothing is selected). It is a page now: the four-square mark the Custom elements button already uses, a heading, one line saying what an element actually is, and the **two routes that exist** — the layer ⋯ menu, and Home → Elements → New element (the draft flow from v9.89). When there IS a selection it offers the button that saves it, right there; when there is not, no button, because a control whose only behaviour is a toast explaining why it did nothing is the "lazy" this is fixing. The search field hides itself when the library is empty — judged on the whole library, not the filtered list, or typing a word that matches nothing would remove the field you typed it into. **Two tests, both mutation-proven, and the mutation check earned its keep twice.** It caught the width assertion running at the suite's 900px, where a media rule gives the field an explicit width and the bug is invisible — the test runs at **380px** now, the only width where the defect exists (v7.79's lesson again: measure the layout you ship to). And the stale-route assertion walks the real Add menu through a new `FM.addMenu._tabs()` seam rather than being told what is in it, so the empty state cannot go back to naming a menu item that has been deleted.
- v9.97 — **A template's clips can be swapped for your own footage — "Insert your Media" (queue 343 (partial), clause 2).** His words, with a screenshot of Alight Motion's version: *"the long term goal for templates is to make it when you press on them you can quickly swap out the media for ur own clips so you can use them as templates and not just the exact same thing as elements"*. **The swap was never the missing part.** `FM.replaceMediaWith` already keeps the layer's transform, keyframes, timing, effects and masks and only re-clamps the trim to the new source's length — which is exactly "it takes that slot's place and keeps the template's timing and effects" — and it is called here rather than re-implemented, so there is no second swap path to keep in step and no new undo story to get wrong. **What was missing was the screen**: a way to see which clips are yours to fill without hunting the timeline for them. Built to his reference rather than to a fresh idea: the template previewing at the top at its own aspect, a scrub bar under it, "Tap to Replace with your Media", a rail of slots — one per replaceable clip, numbered, each showing its duration — and a Replace Media button, with Done in the corner. Tapping a slot **selects** it and seeks the preview to that clip's start, so the second tap is not blind. It opens itself 420ms after a template becomes a project — after the push, not during it, because `body.fm-popping` puts `#app` on a transform and a `position: fixed` child raised mid-push would be re-rooted to it and travel with it. It refuses to appear at all when a template has no video or image layers, because a screen saying "replace your media" over an empty row is worse than no screen. **The slot row is the feature, so that is what the test asserts** — media layers only (a shape and a text layer in the fixture are not yours to replace) and in TIMELINE order, from a deliberately out-of-order fixture, because a row that echoed the layer array would pass a same-order one and still be wrong. **The mutation check rejected the first version of the geometry test and was right twice over.** The gutter assertion — the first slot must not sit flush against the screen edge with its selection ring clipped — passed with the fix removed, because three slots do not overflow the rail and a rail that does not scroll has nothing for `scroll-snap` to snap; it builds twelve now and asserts the overflow itself as a control. (The bug was real and measured: `padding-left` read 14px while `scrollLeft` read 14 at the same moment — snap aligns to the scrollport, which excludes padding, so `scroll-padding` is what makes it respect the gutter.) **And a gate came out of it**: `ship.sh` and `mutate.sh` both read the runner's JSON with `grep -o 'FAIL[^"]*'`, so the first double quote inside a test NAME cuts the failure line short — this one reported itself as `FAILtemplates: \` and the check could not say which assertion had fired. Twelve existing test names carried the same hazard. All renamed, and a suite test now refuses any name containing a double quote, which is cheaper than teaching two shell scripts to parse JSON.
- v9.98 — **The sliders really do stop at their limit, and now there is a test that would notice if they stopped stopping (#347).** His words, with a screenshot of X Skew and Y Skew both pinned at 80.00°: *"Make it so the sliders here and everywhere actually stop when you reach the limit, currently it keeps letting you swipe"*. **This entry had been diagnosed wrong twice, and the second diagnosis was a correction of the first.** Note one said `mtScrub` advanced its ruler offset unconditionally, so a value pinned at its wall still had ticks sliding under the finger — true, and fixed in v9.93. Note two, written while trying to act on note one, said `mtScrub` was the *crop* scrubber and the Skew sliders were built by `tickStrip` — **also wrong**: `js/inspector.js:3595` builds both Skew strips with `mtScrub`, so v9.93's one-line fix was the right fix for the exact control he photographed. Reading the code produced two confident wrong answers in two days, so this pass drove the control instead. **Measured, at 380px, with real pointer events on the Skew strip:** the value climbs 12° a step to −72.00, pins at **−80.00 on step 7**, and the strip's own offset freezes at **−360px on that same step** and never moves again through seven more steps of dragging. It stops dead, which is what he asked for. **"and everywhere" is the other half of his sentence**, so the second ruler kind was driven too — `tickStrip`, the effects-panel slider, which travels by transforming its ruler rather than by moving a background: it walks to −700px and holds there for the last four steps. Between them those two controls are **every slider in the app** (nine sites use one, five the other), and the volume strip is one of the nine. **What is actually new is the guard.** A one-line `if (alive)` is exactly the kind of fix that gets undone by a later refactor with nothing to notice, and this one has already been mis-attributed twice from a code read. The test performs the gesture and judges only what a person can see travel, with a control assertion at each end — the strip must have moved before the wall (or the gesture is not reaching it and the test proves nothing) and must be perfectly still after it. Both halves mutation-checked separately: restoring the unconditional `offset += dx` fails the Skew half, and letting `tickStrip` sync from its unclamped position fails the effects half.
- v9.99 — **"Tuff": seven filters in the TikTok rage-edit style, on his cars — and the new effect they needed (queue 349).** His words: *"Make a filter section called 'tuff' and use the car images for the filters you make… These filters will be good for people who make edits on TikTok that are a tuff style where they use rage rap music etc, kinda dark, just reference TikTok styles on what people do"*. **Blackout, Cold Steel, Bloodline, Static, Nightdrive, Overdrive and Ash** — crushed blacks, contrast up, colour pulled back or driven hard one way, heavy vignette, grain, bloom. Both of the file's authoring rules hold: CSS-filter effects listed first so the rows read in render order, and nothing at an extreme, because Strength fades the whole filter toward the untouched picture. **And the second half of the same request needed a new effect.** *"They should also come with flicker or flash, not in a way that makes the effect flicker on and off but so there's like a black layer on top with not full opacity and has flickering… usually what I do is get a black shape that covers the screen, make opacity like 30% and put a flash or flicker filter on."* He was describing a real gap, not a preference: `flicker`, `blink` and `pulseopacity` all write the ALPHA channel, so they make the LAYER come and go — exactly what he ruled out — and nothing in ~200 effect types modulated BRIGHTNESS over time. **Flash (darken)** multiplies RGB and never touches alpha, so the picture pulses dark while the layer's shape, edges and opacity stay exactly as they were; Depth, Speed, Softness (0 is a hard strobe, 1 a pulse) and Darkest (a floor, so it is a wash rather than a blackout). Deterministic on a stepped time index, hashed the way `flicker` already is, so a preview and an export of the same frame cannot disagree. **It shipped inert on the first pass and the browser said so.** The renderer was written and the registry knew the type, but `POSTFX` — the routing map — did not list it, so nothing ever dispatched: a probe rendering a white rect through it read 255 at every sampled time. Registered now, and measured working (255 → 160/246/225/152/140/135 across six times, alpha 255 throughout). **The cars land here and only here**, which is what v9.82 held them back for: *"I didn't want the car images as the main images for any of the groups but the tuff group… And when you eventually make tuff filters use the cars."* Paired by look rather than by rotation — the darkest shot carries the monochrome grades, the red car at night the warm ones, the bright yellow the two that need something bright to visibly dirty — and checked for repeats across and down at both grid widths. **Two looks were re-authored after looking at them at 380px** rather than after reading the numbers: Blackout needed an explicit brightness pull because "crushed blacks" cannot show on a daylight photo that has barely any, and Static's chromatic aberration came down from 5px to 3 because a preview tile renders at tile size, so an aberration authored for a 1080p frame is proportionally enormous on it and sold rainbow smear instead of a dirty picture. **Tests:** every Tuff filter is built through the real creation path and its surviving effect count compared to what was authored — the library drops unknown types and out-of-range params silently, so a filter can look authored and arrive with nothing in it; each must carry the flash; CSS-first order is asserted per filter. The v9.82 no-cars rule gets the exemption its own comment said it should get, with the converse asserted beside it so an exemption cannot become a hole. And Flash (darken)'s defining property has its own test, which checks ALPHA at every sampled frame and checks it FIRST — `getImageData` un-premultiplies, so an effect that wrongly multiplied alpha would leave RGB at 255 and read as "it never darkened", sending the next person after the wrong bug. Mutation-checked by multiplying alpha too: caught, 1600 pixels.
- v10.00 — **Voronoi Cells are alive (queue 350).** His words: *"Voronoi cells needs the ability to make them move, and I want it to actually move in a cool way and not just a drag it up and down, like they're alive. Because that's what alight motion has"*. It was completely static — two parameters, neither of them time-based, so the pattern was frozen for the whole clip. **The second half of that sentence is the design instruction and it is the part worth getting right**, because the cheap implementation satisfies the first half and is exactly what he ruled out: one Speed slider scrolling the whole field. So the drift is per SEED, not per field. Each cell hashes its index into its own phase and orbits its resting place, with the two axes running at 1 and 0.73 of the same clock — a deliberately non-integer ratio, so they never re-sync and the motion has no visible loop and no direction you could point at. Radius is capped at 0.34 of a grid cell so a seed can never wander out of reach of the 3×3 neighbour search; a seed that escapes its neighbourhood does not make a nicer pattern, it makes a wrong one. **Motion 0 is today exactly, byte for byte** — the offset term is skipped rather than multiplied by zero, and an effect saved before this release has no `motion` param at all, so it reads 0. Measured: 0 pixels differ across three times. **And it costs less than the static version it replaces.** The entry warned about this — Voronoi is already a per-pixel nearest-seed search and an earlier round had to cut a quality maximum that measured 1.2s a frame. The old code hashed both seed offsets INSIDE the pixel loop: nine neighbours × two `Math.sin` × every pixel. Adding two more hashes and two trig calls there would have been four times that, so the seed grid is built once per frame instead (at most ~4k cells) and the pixel loop just reads it. Measured at 240×240: **5.66ms before, 5.32ms after, with the motion on.** **The test pins the clause, not the symptom.** It does not ask whether pixels changed — a sliding sheet passes that. It searches every whole-field shift in a ±16px window and asks how much the best one improves on not shifting at all: a sheet is nearly rescued by its true offset, a field of independent cells is rescued by none. **The mutation check rejected three versions of that assertion and each rejection was a real lesson.** Sixteen cells across a 120px frame makes a shared drift under 2px, which an integer search cannot see (fixed: six cells, ~7px). Comparing t=0 with t=1.8 is 1.08 cycles of a cosine, i.e. almost back where it started (fixed: half a cycle, 0.833s). And the threshold was set by eye at 18 points when the sliding case actually gains 15.5 — so it sat above the thing it was meant to catch. It is 8 now, measured: sliding gains 15.5/15.8/19.7 at three time pairs, alive gains 1.1/2.9/3.2. *(The entry's second clause — the explanation block above the Cells slider — was already done: queue 378 stopped the panel rendering descriptions for every effect, and the text is kept as the browser tooltip and the written record, which is the "somewhere else" he asked for.)*
- v10.01 — **A swipe that starts on a clip now glides like every other swipe (queue 351).** His words: *"Timeline doesn't scrub smoothly when you press on a layer when swiping, this is annoying please add to list"*. The entry said to measure the GESTURE rather than the frame rate, and it was right to: the frame cost of scrubbing has been measured three times and is fine. **A pointerdown on a clip and one on empty lane run down two completely different paths**, and only the empty-lane one sampled a release velocity and released into the momentum glide. So the identical flick either glided or stopped dead depending purely on where your finger happened to land — and on a timeline with layers in it there is barely any empty lane, so the version that stops dead is the one you almost always get. The clip path samples velocity with the same smoothing constants and releases through the same `startMomentum` on the same terms (only if the finger was still travelling when it lifted, so a deliberate settle still lands exactly where you put it). Measured: the same 72px flick now releases at **0.00913 from both**, where the clip one previously recorded nothing at all. Its dead zone came down too — the empty lane commits a scrub at 3px of travel and a clip needed 6, so the first six pixels did nothing and the playhead then took all six at once; it is 4 now, as close as tap-versus-scrub discrimination allows. **Two things the measurement taught, both recorded in the probe:** synthetic pointer events dispatched in one tick all carry the same `timeStamp`, so `dt` is zero, no velocity is ever sampled and BOTH paths report no fling — the first version of the probe did exactly that and reported the bug as absent. And whether a release flung cannot be read off the playhead afterwards, because a glide that is legitimately tiny and one that never started look the same from outside; `FM.timeline._lastFling()` records the release velocity at the one place both paths must come through. Mutation-checked by disabling the new release: caught, "never flung at all".
- v10.02 — **The empty project loses the playhead drawn through its big +, and that + gets real colours (queue 354).** His words, with a phone screenshot of exactly this: *"Hide the player head while the add button is big and also give the plus add button some actual nice colours not just basic blue"*. **The playhead** — the fixed-centre line — ran straight down through the + and through "Tap here to start creating". An empty project has nothing to scrub, so the line was a ruler over a blank page sitting on top of the one control the screen exists for. It is hidden while the big state is up and comes straight back the moment a clip exists, which is asserted too: a rule that just killed the playhead would otherwise pass. The flag goes on `#timeline-panel` rather than on the row, because `#tl-centerline` is a sibling of `#timeline` and a class on the row could never reach it — and it is set in the same line that decides the row is empty, so the two cannot disagree about what "empty" means. **The +** was the slim row's 21px blue glass pill scaled up to 64, and at that size a subtle gradient stops being depth and becomes one flat blue disc. It now carries a conic sweep through the four hues this app already uses to mean "many things" — the Custom elements mark and the add-menu tabs both say it — with the glass highlight kept over the top so it still belongs to the same family as the FAB. Conic rather than linear because a round button wants its colour to travel around it; a linear gradient across a circle always reads as a lit cylinder. **The colour assertion had to be rewritten and the mutation check is why.** The first version counted colour STOPS in the computed background, and the old blue pill is three stops of blue plus a two-stop white highlight — five, which passed. Three shades of one blue is precisely the "just basic blue" he is objecting to, so the question is not how many colours there are but how far apart they sit on the wheel: it converts each stop to a hue, drops anything near white or grey (the glass highlight is white by design), and requires at least three hues more than 40° apart. Caught with the blue pill put back: "1 distinct hue (190°)".
- v10.03 — **Leaving a project stops throwing the desktop layout around (queue 355).** His words: *"There's a glitch at the moment where when I exit out of a project the ui glitches and moves all over the place. Sometimes when entering a project as well. It just makes the app feel slow and buggy and not smooth"*. The entry said to measure a real open→close cycle before touching the animation, and that was the right order: across **59 sampled frames of both directions at 380 and at 1440**, the layout viewport, the document's scroll width and the boxes of `#app`, `#timeline-panel` and `#stage` are all steady. Nothing is being re-laid out mid-flight, which is what the entry suspected. **It is an asymmetry instead, and this file had already written down the reasoning — for the other direction only.** The push is gated to phones, with a comment saying why: it was designed and measured at 380/390/414, and a verifier caught the unscoped version playing the full slide on desktop with `#app` going `position: fixed; z-index: 210` mid-flight at 1280×720, where the Studio layout has its own fixed chrome to collide with. `body.fm-popping #app` sets that same `position: fixed; z-index: 210` — and the pop was never given the same gate. So on a desktop, **leaving a project played exactly the animation that entering one had been gated away from**, which is why exiting is the half he notices. Same gate now, in both directions; the phone keeps its slide and the test asserts that too, because a gate that quietly removed the transition everywhere would otherwise look identical. **And the pop now ends on `animationend`, not only on a timer.** The push has had that since it was written; the pop had a bare `setTimeout` alone. Every one of these keyframes is `animation-fill-mode: both`, so the CLASS is the geometry — leave it on and `#app` stays parked a full viewport away as a fixed box over everything. A timer covers the ordinary case and is throttled to seconds in a backgrounded tab, and coming back to a screen that has "moved all over the place" is precisely the report; the timer stays as the backstop, since `animationend` does not fire on a hidden tab either. Mutation-checked by removing the gate: caught at desktop width.
- v10.04 — **The big + loses its dashed box, and the slim add row finally lines up with the layers (queue 356).** His words: *"when the add button is big and there's nothing on the project get rid of the lines around it, then also when it's small make sure it's centred on its layer a bit better, if you look closely the lines and stuff are just off, going slightly lower than high"*. The first is a one-line change: the dashed outline says "this is a row among others", which is true of the slim row and meaningless when the row IS the whole timeline. Transparent rather than `border: none`, so the box keeps its 1px and nothing inside it shifts by two pixels. **The second was measured before anything was touched, and the measurement moved the diagnosis.** "Slightly lower than high" reads as a centring problem, and the row's CONTENTS were already exact — the + and the label each sat 8.5px from the top of their own box and 8.5px from the bottom, off by 0.00. It was the BOX. **A layer row is 42px with no margin; the add row was 38px with 4px of margin at each end**, so it occupied 46px of the stack while claiming to be a layer — 4px shorter than its neighbours and floating 4px clear of them at each end, which is precisely why its outline could not line up with the rows above and below. (The comment in the stylesheet even described it as "the phone row's 42px-ish", which it was not.) It is 40 + 1 + 1 = 42 now, one layer slot to the pixel, with the 1px margins keeping a hairline between its dashed outline and its neighbours' edges rather than letting them touch. **The test asserts the OUTER slot, not the inner centring** — the inner centring was never broken, so an assertion about it would have gone green on the bug — and it re-checks the centring afterwards anyway, so a "fix" that only stretched the box cannot pass. Both halves mutation-checked separately: the old 38px+4px geometry fails the slot check at 46 against 42, and restoring the dashed colour fails the outline check.
- v10.05 — **A layer can be dragged onto the add row now — it was a hole in the stack (queue 357).** His words: *"currently you can't drag a layer on top of the add layer, it's like they don't think it's there or something"*. He described the model exactly. The reorder drag mapped `.track-row` only, and the add row is deliberately not one — it has no layer and no index, by design, so it can never reach the export or a saved project. **But it occupies a row's worth of the stack**, and every drop position is resolved from `listTop + j * slotH`, i.e. from an assumption that the rows are evenly spaced. So its 42px pushed **every layer beneath it out of step with the model by a whole slot**: nothing opened a gap where it sits, dropping there did nothing, and dropping below it landed a row off. It joins the geometry as a static with no id. It can never be dragged (it is not a layer, so it is never in the drag set) and it is never a drop target in its own right — landing on it resolves to the next real row below, which is the same boundary its own position means, so the two agree instead of competing. It glides with the rows it sits among, because a row that stays put while everything parts around it is exactly the thing the drag cannot see. **And the cleanup was widened with it**, which is the bug this change would otherwise have introduced: the add row now carries `row-part` and an inline transform, and the drop's tidy-up queried `.track-row` alone — it would have stranded the add row wherever the drag left it for the rest of the session. Measured end to end at 380px: the add row shifts on 4 of 4 drag steps where it previously shifted on 0, the rows part correctly around it, dragging the bottom layer up four slots lands it at the top, and nothing is left behind. **The probe needed fixing before the code did**, and it is worth recording: the reorder's listeners live on the ≡ handle, which takes pointer capture — a real browser retargets the moves to it, but a synthetic dispatch on `window` never reaches it, and the first version reported every row motionless, which looks identical to the bug it was hunting. Mutation-checked by putting the `.track-row`-only selector back: caught.
- v10.06 — **The Media and Audio libraries page two rows sideways, and every Add tab opens at the same height (queue 358, correcting queue 299 / v9.47).** His words: *"When I said I wanted the media and audio rows to be only two rows instead of three I didn't mean two rows fitting on screen then you have to scroll down, I just meant two rows solid locked in then you scroll left and right to go to the other rows where the spill over will be"* — and, in the same message: *"they aren't even the same height as the other menus, they need to always open at the same height"*. **Those are one fault, not two.** v9.47 gave the library body `height: auto` plus a two-row `max-height`, which is (a) a vertical scroll window, the exact shape he ruled out, and (b) the reason Media and Audio were the only two tabs overriding the sheet's stated height — so they were also the only two that opened taller than everything else. Deleting the override does both at once: they take the same `clamp(170px, 32vh, 260px)` as Elements, Shape and Template, and the two-row limit moves to where it belongs — the PAGE. The machinery was already sitting beside it; the Shape tab has used this pager for months, so a library tab simply gets a page that holds exactly two rows and the spill-over is one swipe sideways, with page dots underneath. **Measured at 380px across all five tabs: height spread 0px** (every tab 260), Media 2 rows over 2 pages, Audio 2 rows, Shape unchanged at 3 rows over 5 pages. **Two existing tests had to change and both changes are the point rather than collateral.** The queue-299 test asserted the BODY was two rows TALL — that is v9.47's shape, the one he corrected — so it now asserts two rows per PAGE and that the paging is actually exercised. And the card-colour test was reading whichever tab happened to be remembered from the previous render; media tiles are explicitly exempt from its colour assertion, so landing on a library tab left it almost nothing to check and it went red the moment a page held fewer cards. It pins the Elements tab now, which is what it was always about. **The fixture had a lesson too:** a hand-built `FM.mediaLib` stub omitted `getThumb`, the card builder threw, and the test failed for its own reason — which reads exactly like a real failure. It spreads the real library and replaces one method. Mutation-checked by removing the two-row page: caught by both tests.
- v10.07 — **A mask row minimises and swipes away like every other row in the stack (#360 clause 1, partial — the entry stays open).** His words: *"The mask effect… doesn't work like an effect. I can't swipe it away to delete it or minimise it."* **He is right about the history, and the deeper half of it is not the right first move.** A mask is layer STATE (`layer.masks`) rather than a registry effect — that is real, and making it one is a #335-scale migration: 30 call sites across eight files, the render path included. It stays open under that clause with its size written down, so it is a decision rather than a surprise. **Neither thing he actually NAMED needs any of that.** Both came from one place: `masksBlock` rendered every mask fully expanded with no gestures on it, so two masks buried the rest of the panel and there was nothing to swipe. `attachFxGestures` — the wiring behind swipe-left-to-delete and press-hold-to-reorder on effect rows — turned out to be generic already: it reads its list through a two-key `stack` descriptor and deletes by OBJECT IDENTITY rather than by index, so masks take it unchanged with `{ list: l => l.masks, after: afterMasks }`, the same shape the audio stack uses. The row gets the chevron, the grip and the accordion (opening one closes the others, scoped to siblings exactly as the effect stack is). Measured at 380px: collapsed by default, tapping the head opens it, and a left swipe took the layer from **2 masks to 1**. **The one risk was checked BEFORE the change rather than after:** `_expanded` is transient UI state and masks are serialised, so hanging it on a mask could have written a UI flag into his project files. The mask sanitiser rebuilds each mask from a whitelist of eight keys, so it is dropped — and that is now asserted rather than assumed, because a whitelist gaining a passthrough later would silently start saving it. **And the loose end resolved itself into a lesson.** The mutation check caught the change only through this test, but fired on the *open* assertion rather than the swipe one, which made no sense — the head's click handler is attached independently of the gestures. Then the clean suite went red on the same assertion, while the identical probe opened the row happily at 380 AND at 1280 in isolation. It is neither a width problem nor a code bug: `_justReordered()` deliberately swallows any tap within 400ms of a drop, so a row does not open when you release a drag on it, and this test was running milliseconds after the suite's effect-reorder tests. The test waits past that window now. Worth remembering because it presents as both of the things it is not — a layout difference, and a bug in the code under test.

"Empty", Blender's word, repeats Null's mistake of naming an absence. **`layer.type` stays `'null'`**, so this is a string change and every saved project keeps working — asserted, because a rename that quietly moved the data would break files he already has. **The real hazard was the colour, and it is the reason this needed care:** the Add-menu tint table is keyed by LABEL, and "Null being red is good" are his words with that exact value pinned. Renaming the tile without renaming its key would have dropped it silently to the generic ring. Both were renamed together and the red is asserted twice. **The mutation check earned its keep twice more.** Removing the table key did NOT change the colour — there is a curated fallback ring and the card still landed on a red — so that mutation was a bad model of the defect and the real one changes the value instead. And the first version of the new assertion read the icon's computed `color`, which is not where the tint lives; it was DEAD and the check caught it. - v10.23 — **Templates and elements can be duplicated (#374).** His words: *"There's no way to duplicate templates or elements"*. Projects have had Duplicate for a long time — the card's ⋯ menu and the bulk bar both — and these two sibling libraries had `remove()` and nothing else, which is probably why it reads as an oversight rather than a missing feature. Both stores get a `duplicate()`, both card menus get an entry, and the copy is named **"X copy"** to match what projects already do rather than inventing a second convention. **The entry warned of a trap and it turned out not to apply, which is worth stating precisely because the opposite assumption is the expensive one:** "a duplicate MUST re-key `pack.media` or the copy and the original will share media, and deleting one will gut the other" is exactly right for a PROJECT, whose media lives in IndexedDB under the layer's own id — two projects naming the same id genuinely share one record. A pack does not work that way. It carries its media INSIDE the record, IndexedDB structured-clones on put, `remove()` deletes only `tpl:<id>`, and the boot sweep keeps or collects a pack by its INDEX id alone — nothing in it ever consults the layer ids inside. So the copy owns its own clone of every File and is independent by construction, and re-keying would have been motion without meaning (the ids are re-keyed at USE time anyway, by `reIdLayers`). **That reasoning is only safe because it is tested:** the test seeds a real file into the pack, deletes the ORIGINAL, then reads the copy's media back — and mutating the copy to be written without its media reports *"the copy lost media when the original was deleted (1 → 0) — they were sharing records"*. **Two real defects turned up in the same menus:** the element card listed **"Add to the open project" twice**, and the bulk Duplicate button called `FM.projects.duplicate` by name whatever tab was open — so on a template id it would have searched the project store, found nothing and done nothing, which is why it had been hidden behind a `canDuplicate: false` flag instead of fixed. It goes through the tab's own store now. Verified at 375px with the menu open, and the duplicate driven for real from that menu.

What made it identical was the arrangement — a full-width crossbar with an upright dropping from its centre, dividing the frame into a band over two panes, which is AM's glyph. The crossbar stays, because it is the mark that reads as "a layout"; the upright goes, and a single centred rounded block sits beneath it instead. A header over a piece of content, rather than a header over two panes. Three marks either way, so it carries the same weight beside Elements / Shape / Media / Audio, on the same 24×24 grid at the same 1.8 stroke — his own warning was that a tab icon handsome in isolation and wrong next to its neighbours is the queue 313 mistake, so it was judged at 88px **and** at its real 24px with all five side by side (`tests/_tabico.html` renders both rows). What is checkable is checked, and what is not is written down.)* **The timeline + only.** v10.30 made the home + share this exact ramp, so animating both looked obvious — but `#hm-new` has no pseudo-element left: its ::before is the 82px hit-box ring and its ::after is the glint sheen. The highlight could not ride on the spinning disc either — a highlight that turns reads as the light source moving, not the paint — so it now has its own static layer above the disc. - v10.38 — **A clip that decodes slowly is no longer written off forever (#399).** His words: *"I keep getting an issue where I add a clip and make an edit but then load it again and it says my browser can't decode the image then the video goes blank. Probably won't be an issue when we make it an app so it's not a huge deal."* **The shape of the report is what found it, and the message was a red herring.** Adding the clip works; reloading it goes blank — and an unsupported codec fails *both* times, so the "can't decode" toast was not describing the real fault. `FM.wireVideoRepaint` gives a video 15 seconds to produce a frame, then marks the record `undecodable` and says so; the compositor SKIPS an undecodable record, which is the blank video. **And nothing could ever lift that mark:** the handler that clears it opened with `if (settled) return`, and the timeout sets `settled` — so a `loadeddata` landing a moment after the deadline hit that early return and the record stayed condemned for the life of the session. **What makes a reload different is exactly what trips it:** on hydrate every video in the project decodes from cold at once, so on a phone one of them can outrun a budget a single warm import never came near. The verdict can now be overturned by the evidence arriving late — the listeners are still attached, and a frame at any point clears the mark and asks for a repaint. Driven in the test on a real `<video>` with a stubbed readyState and a 60ms budget, so the race runs for real instead of being asserted about; the mutation that restores the early return reports *"the frame arrived and the clip is still marked undecodable"*. **He was also wrong to discount this one**, and that is worth saying: it is work going blank between sessions, and "it'll be fine once it's an app" would have shipped this code into the wrapper unchanged.
- v10.39 — **The filter tiles raster at the screen's resolution instead of a fixed 2× (#400).** His words: *"The filters could use a quality bump, currently they're very low res and I think that makes them look un appealing."* It was a DPR mismatch rather than a design problem: the tiles were rasterised at a fixed 2× and his phone is 3×, so every one was drawn at two thirds of the resolution it is displayed at and then upscaled by the browser. The raster now follows the screen — floored at 2 so nothing regresses on a 1× display, capped at 3 so a 4× screen cannot quietly quadruple a queue of ~200 tiles. Verified by running the app headlessly at `--force-device-scale-factor=3`: the tile really does come out 228×174 (39,672px) against 152×116 (17,632px). **`R` itself is deliberately untouched**, which is the restraint that makes this safe: the note at the top of that file measured the all-effects worst case at ~163MB of cached canvas at 288², and 3× would take it past 360MB — only the 76×58 filter tiles moved, which is 2.25× of something small. **The timing measurement the entry asked for cannot be taken headlessly, and no number is reported rather than a number I do not trust:** timing the queue's drain measures the harness, because the queue is rAF-driven and rAF is throttled under a virtual clock; timing the raster directly returns 0.00ms because `performance.now()` does not advance under it either. **The cost answer is structural, and it is a better one than a stopwatch:** each rAF slice is bounded to 8ms, so a bigger tile cannot lengthen a frame — it can only make the queue take more frames to drain, and the first paint the entry was protecting is protected by that budget rather than by the tile size. The rule is tested as a pure function of dpr, so it can be checked without a 3× screen to check it on, and the tile box is asserted to actually use it — a correct rule wired to nothing looks exactly like a fix.

The test caught it on the first run. Closing at pointerdown and stopping the event there means the tap is consumed by the thing it dismisses. **The "but not the layer" half is the whole request:** the phone's inspector sheet is derived from the selection, so deselecting closes everything and you have to find the layer again to carry on. The exit goes through the browser's own path, so a tap-away **applies** the picks rather than binning them — that is #389, and a tap-away is an exit like any other. The test asserts both halves, because a check that only watched the menu close would pass with his actual complaint fully intact: the menu closed either way. Mutation-checked by removing the `stopPropagation()` — it reports *"the tap closed the menu AND dropped the layer"*.
