Worth admitting: the first version of this file decoded perfectly, reported the right size and length, raised no error, and never played a single frame. It was only caught by playing the old file next to it.
- v11.31 — **every open item in your requests file now says, on its first line, whether it is waiting on me or on you.** You asked for labels and no deleting — *"don't clean up unless it's just labeling stuff for quick finding"* — so nothing has been removed or shortened; each open entry just gained one line at the top: READY, NEEDS YOU, HELD, BIG, NOTE or LATER. The labels are generated rather than typed, and regenerate every time anything ships, because a status written by hand is accurate the day it is written and quietly misleading a week later — it would still say "waiting on you" long after you had answered. Writing it turned up something worse than untidiness: **five of your requests had gone invisible**, and by my own hand. The tool that decides what can be worked on treats the phrase "standing instruction" as "nothing to build here", and when I logged your answers I wrote "his standing instruction of the same day" into five entries — the rainbow Create buttons, the export formats, the tilt keyframes, the template icon and the elements menu. All five silently dropped off the list of things I could pick up. They are back, and the rule is fixed so a note about a request can no longer bury the request. The count of things ready to work on went from 19 to 24.
- v11.32 — **a clip can no longer be dragged off into empty space past the end of your project.** Your words: *"Found a glitch where when you drag a layer to the right too far it breaks the project timeline"*, and with the screenshot, *"it just keeps going past the timeline"*. There was a limit stopping a clip being dragged off the LEFT end and nothing at all stopping it going right — so a clip could be pushed as far as you had patience for, stranded out in empty space, with the ruler and the scrollable width politely growing to follow it. The rule now is that a clip cannot start later than the end of your project as it was when you picked it up. Moving a clip to the end and making the project longer still works exactly as before — that is how a project grows — but one drag can no longer open a gap bigger than the whole project. Two things were deliberate. When several clips are selected they stop **together**: if any one of them would go past the end, the whole selection stops there, because stopping them one at a time is how a selection silently changes its own spacing — a bug this timeline has had before. And a clip that is ALREADY out past the end, in a project made before today, is never yanked backwards when you touch it; moving your work without being asked would be worse than the original problem.
- v11.33 — **Rotation, X tilt and Y tilt now keyframe independently.** Your words, with all three readouts and the diamond circled: *"The key frames for these three things are all interacting with each other and causing issues, make em independent"*. They were already three separate settings — each number box only ever wrote its own. What they shared was the diamond button beside them, which keyframes everything in the panel at once. That is right for position, where X and Y are two halves of one thing, and wrong for these three, which are independent axes that merely share a panel. So a layer sitting at a 20° tilt would have that tilt turned into an animation the moment you keyframed a spin, and clearing a spin keyframe took the tilt's with it. Now: keyframing rotation keys rotation. The tilt stays exactly where it was — still 20°, just not animated. Two things were deliberately preserved. A tilt you have ALREADY animated is still keyed alongside, because dropping it would strand a real animation half-finished. And position keyframing is untouched — X, Y and a non-default Z still travel together, which is the behaviour that makes moving things work. There is also a finer control you may not have noticed: tapping a row's NAME picks that one property, and the diamond then keys only that row.
- v11.34 — **the Media and Audio tabs in the Add sheet no longer leave a big empty band underneath.** Your words, with the screenshot: *"fill it but those tabs are still broken as per attached image"*. Those two tabs have three buttons where Elements has nine, and since every add menu was made the same tall height (which you asked for), three buttons sat huddled along the top of a tall box with about 196 pixels of nothing beneath them — which is what looked broken from across a room. The obvious fix, stretching that single row to fill the space, was tried before and measured: it produced a 113-wide, 260-tall sliver, which is worse than the gap. So instead a sparse tab now drops from three columns to two, and the same three buttons fill the sheet as two proper rows — bigger, squarer targets at the exact proportions the earlier measurements picked out as the good ones, with the odd one out spanning the full width so the grid ends flush instead of with a hole in the corner. Elements and Shape are untouched. There is a check on this now that measures the leftover space on both tabs, and it starts by proving it can see a tab that already fills — otherwise "no empty space" would also be the reading you get from a sheet that never opened.
- v11.35 — **the speed slider moves in 5% steps instead of jumping ten times speed at once.** Your words: *"The speed slider goes WAY too fast, it goes up 10x at a time, slow this way the fuck down"* — and "10x at a time" turned out to be literally, arithmetically exact. Every ruler in the app automatically coarsens its steps so it never ends up thousands of notches long. That is sensible for a normal setting, and it went badly wrong here: when the speed range was widened so you could reach 1000× (which you asked for), that automatic coarsening quietly took the step from 5% to 1000% — one notch of your finger, ten times faster. Worse, the note in the code right beside it still promised "the ruler still moves 5% per step so ordinary speeds feel exactly as they did". That promise was true the day it was written and was broken later by a change two hundred lines away, and nothing failed to say so. The speed row now insists on its own 5% step, so a small drag makes a small change and 1.5× or 2× are things you can actually land on. The full 1000× is still there and still reached by typing in the box, exactly as before. Every other slider in the app is untouched, which the check now proves rather than assumes.
- v11.36 — **the export button is not a rainbow any more.** Your words: *"Also I never wanted a rainbow export button change it back to what it was"*. It was never a decision — it was a leftover. The export buttons used to sit at the front of the same CSS rule that carried the app's plain glass finish, shared by most chrome buttons. When the home + was turned into the coloured disc you asked for, that rule's contents were replaced and the export buttons were simply left listed on it, so they quietly became rainbow discs too. Nothing broke and nothing warned; the rule just kept painting whoever was still named on it. Export goes back to the tinted glass and accent glow it had before, and the two + buttons keep their disc. One thing that had to change with it: the arrow is drawn in whatever colour the button says, and that had been set to near-black to read against a bright rainbow — removing the rainbow on its own would have left a black arrow on dark glass. Taking a colour off a button turned out to be two changes, not one, and the check now measures the arrow's brightness as well as the button's paint.
- v11.37 — **the Save and Discard buttons in the cog menu work again — and the reason they did not is a mistake I made and shipped.** You reported them doing nothing. They did nothing because there were two of them. A bad edit of mine eleven releases ago, while removing the project presets, was meant to delete a section of the page and instead **copied** one — leaving thirty-one duplicated ids, including complete second copies of the canvas settings dialog and the export dialog. When a page has two elements with the same name, the app only ever finds the first, so every button handler attached itself to the invisible copy and the one you were actually pressing was dead. That is also why the cog menu was showing "Discard" and "Save" at all — those belong to the export card, and it had inherited them. The page has been rebuilt from the last good version with the preset removal redone properly, so it is back to one of everything: the cog menu has App settings / Cancel / Apply, and Discard / Save are back on the export card. The part that matters more than the fix: this shipped through eleven releases with every test passing, because nothing had ever checked for it — a duplicate is invisible, nothing crashes, one copy is just quietly dead. There is now a check that fails the moment any name appears twice anywhere in the app.
- v11.38 — **opening a project is two moves now, not one blur.** Your words: *"I want it so the project swipes to the left first with a smooth animation that is well designed, and then after it does the swipe to the left the project opens from the right smoothly and slowly, currently it's very cutty and they move at the same time and it's just off"*. Both halves of that were true. The project was starting to arrive the moment it had finished loading — which on a big project is fine, because the list is still travelling and you never see the join, but on a small one that is a few tens of milliseconds, so the two motions ran on top of each other and the whole thing read as a single cut. The arrival now waits for the list to finish leaving, so you get the swipe left, then the project coming in, in that order, every time regardless of how fast the project loads. And the arrival is slower than the departure — 520ms against 380ms — on an easing that decelerates into place rather than stopping dead, because a thing leaving can accelerate away but a thing arriving should settle. The card you tapped still leaves the instant you touch it, which matters: an earlier release deliberately fixed a fifth of a second of dead screen there and this does not undo it — something is moving at every moment, the two things simply no longer move at the same time. One trap worth noting: the little + orb rides along with the editor and had its own copy of the timing, so slowing the editor alone would have left the orb arriving 140ms early on a different path. They now read from one shared setting.
- v11.39 — **every effect category has its own icon now, instead of just a colour and a word.** Your words: *"Make an icon for each section that resembles the overall theme in some way, like for colouring you could do an interesting colour palette but do something distinct for each one"*. Twelve icons, each drawn for what its section actually does: a painter's palette for Colouring (your example), one sharp circle beside one that has gone soft for Blur, a straight grid pushed out of true for Warping, a spark and scattered dots for Generative, a cut gem for Stylize, a pen nib for Drawing / Edge, a shape held still while its edges get thrown about for Shakes / Movement, the same tile four times for Repetition, a figure standing inside a frame for Keying, a panel solid down one side and see-through down the other for Opacity, a letter for Text, and a plane with depth for 3D. They are drawn in the same weight and size as the icons on the Add menu tabs so they look like part of the app rather than borrowed, and deliberately none of them is a cube — the Elements tab already owns that shape. The tile colours are unchanged; the icon is what tells you what the section is. There is a check that every category has one and that no two are the same, because a single shared fallback glyph would pass "they all have icons" while leaving them exactly as hard to tell apart as before.
- v11.40 — **the Faves control is a proper gold button instead of a thin notch.** Your words, with it circled: *"Make the faves menu a big button and not just this small notch, and give it some nice shiny golden background colours"*. It was a transparent full-width strip with a four-pixel grab bar and a line of small caps — about thirty pixels tall with no surface of its own, which is why it read as a divider rather than something to press. It is now a full-width gold button with the star that marks a favourite on every tile, the count, and the chevron. "Shiny" is three layers rather than one flat fill: a warm ramp for the metal, a soft highlight across the top third for the light, and a hairline inner rim so the edge catches — a single flat gold would have read as a sticker stuck on. The colour is the one already in the app: the same gold as the ★ you tap to favourite something, so the button and the things it collects match instead of introducing a new accent. The small grab bar stays above it, because you can also pull that strip down to open faves and taking away its only visible hint would have hidden a feature.
- v11.41 — **filter sections are one row you swipe, instead of two rows stacked up.** Your words, with the TUFF section photographed: *"Make in the filters menu for rows like tuff where there's two lines just one line and you scroll left and right swiping to see the others"*. The sections were a four-across grid, so TUFF's eight filters wrapped onto a second line and that one section cost twice the height of every other — pushing the rest of the list off the bottom of the screen, which is what your screenshot shows. Each section is now a single row you swipe sideways: same tiles, same size, the extras just live off to the right and settle neatly when you let go. Sections that already fit — four or fewer — look and behave exactly as before, so only the long ones changed. On a desktop, where there is no swipe, the row keeps a slim scrollbar; on touch it stays clean. It reuses the same sideways-rail behaviour the font picker in the text editor already had, rather than inventing a second kind of scroller that would drift away from it later.
- v11.42 — **filters work like the effects menu now: tap to select, then press Add.** Your words: *"When adding filters make it so that you can toggle them select and then have to press add, like the main effects menu, this is good so I can see them all quickly and not have to add then delete and go back. And so you can add multiple at once if you're heart desires"*. Tapping a filter used to apply it there and then AND throw you back to the stack, so trying three looks meant add, look, delete, go back — three times over. Now a tap just marks it, with the same numbered badge the effects menu uses, and a bar appears at the bottom saying how many you have picked. Nothing touches your layer until you press it. Tap a marked one again to unmark it and the rest renumber. Press Add and they all go on at once, in the order you numbered them — which matters, because filters stack and the order changes the result. The badge and the button are the effects menu's own, not lookalikes, so the two menus count and read the same instead of drifting into two dialects of the same idea. An existing check that used to say "tapping a filter adds it" has been updated rather than deleted: the half it was really guarding — that you land back on the stack with the new filter open — is still true and still checked, just after the Add instead of after the tap.
- v11.43 — **the stairs button is two buttons now, one going down and one going up.** Your words, with it circled and a line drawn down the middle: *"Split this button into two, one stairs down and one stairs up."* The button lines several selected clips up end to end, each starting where the last one finished — and its icon is three steps descending to the right, which matched what it did: the top clip went first and the chain stepped downward. There was no way to ask for the opposite. Now there is. Worth being precise about what "up" means, because there are two ways to make a chain climb and only one of them is safe: it starts from the BOTTOM clip and works back, it does not reverse your layers. Your stack stays exactly as you arranged it and only the timings move, which the check enforces — three clips of one, two and three seconds go 0 / 1 / 3 pressing down and 0 / 3 / 5 pressing up, with the layer order untouched both times. On PC the two of them share one row rather than taking one each, and that came out of a measurement: a fourth full-width row dropped every button in that panel from 48px to 34px, thinner than the same strip on your phone, which is the "make them big" complaint from a while back coming back through a different door. Side by side they cost one row between them, everything stays 48px, and it says the true thing about them — they are one control split down the middle, which is how you described it. On the phone it is four equal buttons in the one strip, 81px each at 380px with nothing cut off.
- v11.44 — **Pitch Shift can be keyframed now, and it glides.** Four of the six audio sliders you asked about are done. This one turned out to be the cheapest of them, not the dearest: the other three had to be rescued with a bank of crossfading shapers because you cannot ramp a transfer curve, but Pitch Shift never had a curve. Everything its knob touches was already a real, schedulable audio value — the setter was just slamming each one in immediately and throwing away the "when" that told it to happen later, so all thirty values a second landed at once and the last one won. It schedules them properly now. No extra machinery, nothing to warn you about. One deliberate choice worth knowing: dragged by hand the slider still steps in whole semitones, but an ANIMATED one slides through the in-between values, so a rise from 0 to 12 is a smooth glide instead of twelve audible jumps — and it still hits the exact whole numbers at your keyframes. Measured against the app's own audio chain: a 220 Hz tone held at +12 comes back at 439 Hz, and a keyframed 0 → 12 over four seconds passes 257 Hz at one second and 366 Hz at three, both within 1.5% of the notes they should be. The check also proves a plain, un-keyframed Pitch Shift does none of that extra work — the same trap the Distortion version fell into, where every clip in every project quietly paid for animation it wasn't using. **Still to come: Reverb Size and Reverb Decay**, the two that rebuild a whole room and are genuinely expensive; those are the ones that will get the warning you asked for.
- v11.45 — **every effect slider in the app can be keyframed now. All of them.** This finishes the oldest thing on your list — *"each effect slider having its own key frames still doesn't exist fully"* — and it is worth saying plainly: 499 of 499 visual sliders and **60 of 60 audio ones**, with none left out. Reverb's Size and Decay were the last two, and the hardest, because a reverb's setting isn't a number — it's a whole room, recorded as sound. You can slide a number while the audio plays. You cannot slide a room. Worse, when the app renders your export it has to build the entire sound graph before it starts, and never gets another chance to change it partway through — so "swap the room when the slider moves" isn't something that can be done at all. What happens instead: the app looks at where your keyframes actually are, builds each of the rooms your animation passes through, and fades between them. The fade is done in a way that keeps the volume steady through each hand-over — done naively there's a dip at every one, which you'd hear as a pumping right in the middle of the sweep you wanted smooth. Measured: closing a room from 6 seconds down to 0.4 lands exactly on a plain 0.4-second room, and a sweep between near-identical rooms stays within 2.6% of a steady one the whole way. **And the warning you asked for is there** — *"if audio key frames break the project and lag too much just put a warning next to it before use"*. It sits under Size and Decay, and only once you've actually keyframed one, because a warning that's always on is wallpaper. These two earned it: they're genuinely the expensive pair. The other four didn't, so they don't have one. Two things that cost nothing, deliberately: a plain un-animated Reverb builds none of this and renders exactly as it always did, and a decay that drifts from 2.0 to 2.004 is treated as one room, because that isn't a change anyone can hear.
- v11.46 — **Text to Voice, in the spot you drew it.** Your words: *"Where I outlined add a button that says text to voice and make a whole menu and feature for this"* — and then, when I said the hard part might be impossible, *"if this is too hard then don't do it but atleast a simple option for me to test"*. This is that. On a text layer there's now a **Text to Voice** button in the strip right under the clip, above the trim/split three, exactly where you circled. It opens a menu that shows the words it's about to read, lets you pick from every voice your device has (180 on this Mac, all of them offline — Karen, the Australian one, is the default), and gives you speed and pitch. Press Play and it reads your text out loud. **Now the part I'm not going to dress up.** It plays on your device, and it will *not* be in an exported video. That isn't laziness or a shortcut — the browser will happily speak text but gives no way whatsoever to capture what it said, so there's no sound file to put on the timeline. No browser offers this; it isn't something I can work around. The menu says so on screen rather than letting you find out after you've built something around it. So this is genuinely the "simple option to test" you asked for, not the TikTok version. **Getting a voice into an actual export needs one of two things, and both are your call:** a cloud voice service — which sounds far better but means an API key, a small bill, and your text leaving the device, which breaks this app's whole local-only promise — or recording a voiceover yourself, which is completely local, already lands on the timeline as normal audio, and involves no robot voice at all. Tell me which and I'll build it. Everything you set is saved with the project, and anything odd in a saved file is checked before it reaches the speech engine.
- v11.47 — **Text to Voice was forgetting your chosen voice. Fixed.** Found by looking for bugs rather than by you hitting it, and it was mine — a week-old mistake in the version that added the feature. What happened: pick a voice, close the project, reopen it, and touch the Speed slider straight away — your voice was quietly reset to the device default. Changing one setting wiped another you hadn't touched, which is the worst kind of small bug because nothing tells you. The cause is a genuinely sneaky bit of browser behaviour: the list of available voices doesn't exist yet when a page opens — it arrives a moment later. The code was reading your saved voice by looking it up in that list, so during those first moments it found nothing, decided you hadn't chosen one, and saved that over your real answer. Now your choice is kept as your choice, and it's only matched against the installed voices at the one moment a voice actually has to be handed to the speech engine. Two smaller things went with it: pressing Play in that same early moment used to read your line in the wrong voice without saying so, and now it waits the extra beat; and pressing Stop during that wait no longer lets it start speaking afterwards anyway. Nothing else about the feature changed, and an unrecognised voice name still falls back safely.
- v11.48 — **a damaged project file can no longer import as an empty-looking project.** Another one found by looking for bugs rather than by you hitting it. The project's own settings — size, frame rate, length — have been checked on import for a long time, but each individual layer's *timing* never was. So if a file arrived with a layer whose length wasn't actually a number — corrupted in transit, hand-edited, half-written by a crash — that nonsense went straight into the project. Everything that positions a clip works out where it ends by adding its length to its start, and adding a number to nonsense gives nonsense, so the clip silently never drew and the whole project reported itself as zero seconds long. Nothing crashed and nothing was said; the project just looked empty. That's the worst way for a file to fail, because it looks like your work is gone. Now a layer's start and length are always real numbers, clamped to something sensible, and a file like that opens with the clip intact instead of vanishing. This matters more from here on: you've asked to be able to send people your projects and templates, and the moment that exists, "a file I made" becomes "a file someone sent me". Two things deliberately left alone — a speed or volume you've *keyframed* is untouched, because turning that back into a plain number would quietly delete your animation, and a perfectly good project comes through completely unchanged, which the check enforces exactly.
- v11.49 — **an animation in a damaged project file no longer quietly stops being an animation.** Same family as the last one, found the same way — by hunting rather than by you hitting it. The app stores each moving setting as a list of keyframes in time order, and everything that reads them trusts that order. Everything FreeMotion itself writes is in order, so this can't happen from normal use. But a file that's been corrupted, hand-edited, or half-written by a crash can arrive with them shuffled — and when that happened, the whole animation silently collapsed to a single frozen value. Not an error, not a warning: your movement was just gone, with nothing to undo. There was a second, quieter version too, where a keyframe with no value at all could put a layer somewhere it was never meant to be. Both are repaired on the way in now — shuffled keyframes are put back in order, incomplete ones are dropped, and if nothing usable is left the setting simply stops pretending to be animated. The repair reaches everywhere animation lives — position, speed, volume, every visual effect and every audio effect — because it looks for the shape of an animation rather than working from a list of places to check, so anything that becomes animatable later is covered automatically. Two things deliberately protected: **animated colours survive**, since those are stored as words rather than numbers and a careless rule would have deleted every one of them, and a perfectly good project comes through completely untouched, which the check enforces exactly.
- v11.50 — **a template could create a project your phone cannot open — twice over. Fixed.** This is the most serious thing the recent bug hunts have turned up, so it's worth explaining. Projects have a size limit for a hard reason: a canvas far beyond it needs about a gigabyte of memory, which iPhones simply refuse. The app has checked that limit for a long time. But starting a new project **from a template** slipped past it: the check ran, and then the very next step replaced the whole project with the template's own settings, throwing the checked version away. An oversized template landed in your editor at full size and was immediately saved to disk that way. That's the nasty part — it wouldn't just crash once. Because it becomes your current project, it would crash again every time you opened the app, with no obvious way back in. Two fixes, and the second is the one that matters most: the template path now re-checks after it builds the project, **and every project re-checks its size whenever it opens**. So anything already saved in a bad state repairs itself on the way in rather than taking the app down. Your ordinary projects are completely unaffected — a 1080×1920 at 60fps opens as exactly that, which the check enforces. Worth adding: the layers inside templates were already being checked properly, so this was only ever about the project's own settings. And this matters more the moment you start sending templates to other people, which you've asked for.
- v11.51 — **the last trace of "canvas presets" is gone.** You put your foot down on this: *"presets are just for effects not anything else, if it says preset remove any other function than just saving what effects the layer has."* The visible feature went at the time, but a piece of it was left behind in the code — a function that built a canvas "preset" out of your aspect, size, frame rate and background, sitting under a comment block headed *Canvas presets*. Nothing called it any more, so it changed nothing you could see, but it was still there with your word on it, waiting to be re-wired by anyone reading that comment. Removed. Found by re-auditing every request against the actual code rather than trusting the notes, after you told me I'd missed a lot — which you had, and this was one.
- v11.52 — **🚨 the export frame rate was silently 30, whatever your project was.** This is the one worth reading. The export dialog's frame-rate list is supposed to open on **"Same as project"** — the comment in the code has said so for months. It didn't. Two rungs in that list were both marked as the default, and when that happens the browser takes the lower one, which was **30 fps**. So unless your project happened to be at an unusual rate, opening Export showed "30 fps" and rendered at 30 — a 60fps project quietly halved, a 50 or 25fps project quietly changed — with nothing on screen telling you. The fix is one stray word removed from the page. It survived this long precisely because the note above it described the correct behaviour, so anyone checking read the explanation and moved on. There's now a test that reads the markup itself rather than the intention. Found by re-checking every past request against the actual code after you told me I'd missed things — you were right, and this was the most expensive one.
- v11.53 — **opening Canvas settings on a 24fps project used to change it to 30.** Another one found by re-checking your old requests against the code rather than trusting the notes. You once told me: *"drop 24, keep 25, add 15 and 120"* for the frame-rate lists. The lists changed — but a second, hidden copy of that list inside the code didn't, and it still believed 24 was an option and that 15 and 120 weren't. So on a **24fps project**, opening Canvas settings showed a **blank** frame-rate box, and pressing Apply read that blank as nothing and wrote **30fps** over your project. Just looking at the settings destroyed the setting. Meanwhile 15fps and 120fps projects opened on "Custom…" instead of their own rows, which was untidy but harmless. Fixed by deleting the hidden copy entirely — the dialog now asks the actual list what rows exist, so the two can never disagree again. Checked across every rate the app supports: 24 opens on "Custom… 24" and stays 24, 15 and 120 land on their own rows, and nothing gets rewritten.
- v11.54 — **the export settings stopped quietly disagreeing with your project.** Your rule for these two was that the settings cog owns the frame rate and the size, and anything you change on the export screen is a one-off for that render. The code even said so in its own notes. It wasn't doing it. Two ways: pick 60fps for one export, then change the project to 50 in the cog — reopening Export still said 60, because the reset only ran for unusual frame rates and skipped every common one. And worse with resolution: what got remembered wasn't a size, it was a *ratio*. Pick 720p on a 1080×1920 project, then resize your canvas to 2160×3840, and Export came back showing "1440p" — a resolution you never picked, on a project it was never picked for. Both now start from your project every single time you open the dialog, exactly as you asked. Off-ladder rates like 48fps still work, which is what the old code was really protecting.
- v11.55 — **you can finally type a frame rate when exporting.** Your words, a while back: *"if you made a custom fps or other things etc there's no way to export at that."* Half of that got built — Export gained a **Custom size…** for the resolution — and the frame-rate half never did. So the rate could only ever be one of the fixed rungs or "Same as project", which meant a 30fps project could not be rendered out at 24 by any route at all (and 24 had already been dropped from every list). The frame-rate menu now ends with **Custom…**, and picking it reveals a box you type into, starting from your project's own rate so it's never blank. It's clamped to 1–120 like the canvas settings, an empty or silly value falls back to your project's rate, and it deliberately isn't remembered next time — the settings cog owns the frame rate, and an export change is a one-off for that render, which is the rule you set. Checked at phone width: the new row lines up with the rest of the dialog and is the same size as every other control.
- v11.56 — **your default shape colour now actually applies to drawings.** You asked for a home setting that picks the colour new shapes start as. It worked for shapes added from the menu — but freehand and vector **drawings ignored it completely** and always came out white, even though the note against that request claimed it "reaches every route that spawns a shape, including freehand and vector drawing". It didn't; the drawing tool had white written into it directly. Now the pencil opens in your colour, the swatch in the drawing bar shows it, and the finished drawing keeps it. Two things left deliberately alone: if your setting is "random" the tool still starts white, which is what it has always done, and a colour you pick by hand in the drawing bar still wins and stays picked — a default is where you start, not something that overrules you every time you open the tool. Found by re-checking your past requests against the code after you told me things had been missed.
- v11.57 — **trimming a clip now lands exactly on a frame.** This is the groundwork for the request you made on 14 August that I'd never even started, because it had gone missing in the file: *"the notches are frames and the whole thing has to actually line up with the notches."* You were describing what Alight Motion shows while you drag a clip edge, and that sentence turns out to be the important half. Trimming already moved in whole-frame steps — but a whole-frame *step* from an edge that isn't on a frame keeps it off the grid for ever, and an imported clip's length is whatever the file happens to be, never a neat number. So dragging an edge could only ever land between notches. Now the edge itself is rounded to the nearest frame, so where you drop it is a real frame. Snapping to another clip still wins when it's active, and only the edge you're actually dragging moves — the other end stays put. The visible half of your request, the readout and the notch strip with the landing notch filled in, is next; it would have been drawing a promise the trim couldn't keep until this was true.
- v11.58 — **dragging a clip edge now tells you what you're doing, with the frame notches.** This is the rest of the request from 14 August that had gone missing in the file. Your words: *"it tells you all of this information and also shows on little notches, by colouring in the exact notch it will land on, because the notches are frames and the whole thing has to actually line up with the notches."* While you drag a clip's edge, a small panel appears above it with six numbers in two rows: **Start · End · Duration** on top — where the clip sits on the timeline — and **In · Out · Change** below, where In and Out are the points *inside the source footage*, and Change is signed so you can see exactly how far you've pulled. Under them is a strip of frame notches with the one you're about to land on lit up in the middle, every fifth notch drawn slightly stronger so you can count, and pink/green marks for the clip's own start and end when they're in view. Two deliberate choices: a shape or text layer shows a dash for In and Out rather than inventing numbers, because it has no source footage; and the notch strip is a window *around the edge you're dragging* rather than the whole clip — my first attempt drew the whole clip, which meant the edge was always at one end and the highlighted notch told you nothing at all.
- v11.59 — **you can pinch to zoom and pan while drawing — and pinching no longer leaves ink.** You asked for this a while back: *"another option that lets you grab the screen and zoom in or out so you can do more detailed drawing."* Earlier work made the tool keep whatever zoom you'd already set, but the actual gesture was never built, so the only way to pan was a mouse wheel — which is no way at all on a phone. Worse than that, and this is the part I'd want to know about: putting a second finger down didn't just fail to zoom, it **drew**. The second finger ran through the ordinary drawing path and committed a stroke, so every attempt to pinch left a mark on your drawing. Now two fingers pan and zoom together, anchored so the canvas stays under your fingers, and the half-drawn stroke is thrown away rather than committed. One finger still draws exactly as before — that's checked, because a fix that turned every touch into a gesture would be far worse than the bug. The canvas also can't be flung off-screen: the same guard the wheel pan already had is now shared by both rather than copied, since a second copy of a rule is what caused three separate bugs this week.
- v11.60 — **the Sound effects card got its white edge back on PC.** A while ago you asked for that card to have a bright gradient outline, and it was built — but a later change gave every card in the PC panel a glow that follows your cursor, and the two were quietly fighting over the same slot. The cursor glow won, so on desktop that card ended up with **no outline at all** (its own border is deliberately invisible, because the gradient ring was supposed to be the edge). On your phone it still looked right, which is why it went unnoticed. The two effects now have a slot each, so the card has its white edge at rest *and* still lights up toward your cursor like its neighbours — on both layouts.
- v11.61 — **the "move" and "extend" buttons for multiple clips are finally telling apart.** You said these two looked the same, with *"a couple of pixels of ink"* between them. That got fixed — twice — but only ever for the version you see with ONE clip selected. The pair you get with several clips selected still had the original drawings: a closed box, and the same box open at one edge. Now they match the fixed pair: **move** is a solid filled block sliding to the playhead, **extend** is an outlined box reaching out with a dashed line. A difference you can see instantly rather than one you have to squint for. Found by re-reading your old requests against the code — the complaint was fixed in one place and quietly left alone in the other.
- v11.62 — **four places were still calling a controller a "null".** You had that layer renamed a while back because "null" means nothing to anyone — the Add menu says **Controller** now. But four other places never got the memo: the right-click menu on the timeline, two messages in the effects browser explaining why effects and masks can't apply, and the keyboard-shortcuts sheet. All four now say controller. Nothing about your saved projects changes — the app still records the layer as the same thing internally, so every project you've made keeps working; this was only ever about the words you read. There's now a check that fails if the old word reappears anywhere on screen, which the original request had actually asked for and never got.
- v11.63 — **the Outline toggle on videos and photos actually draws an outline now.** You asked for outlines to be available on videos and clips, not just shadows. The controls arrived — the Outline & Shadows card offers the toggle, a colour, a size and a position on any video or image — but **none of it drew anything**. The part that turns your toggle into an actual outline was written correctly and simply never consulted for ordinary clips; it was only ever reached for caption tracks and for the live preview when you're browsing effects. So the whole card sat there looking functional and did nothing. Now it draws, follows the colour and size you set, hugs the visible shape of the clip (so a cropped or rounded one gets an outline around what you can actually see), and switches cleanly off. The check counts real pixels rather than asking the code whether it thinks it's working — because the translation *was* always correct, and a test that only asked it would have passed happily throughout.
- v11.64 — **the rotation keyframe button could delete your tilt animation in one press.** You reported that rotation, X tilt and Y tilt were "all interacting with each other and causing issues". Part of that was fixed a while back, and the notes told you the rest was too — but only when you'd first tapped one of the three rows to single it out, which is not how it starts. Left alone, the diamond on the left rail looked at **all three** channels to decide what it was going to do. So if your tilt had a keyframe where the playhead sat but rotation didn't, the button quietly turned into a **delete** button: one press wiped that tilt keyframe — flattening the animation — and never keyed rotation at all, which is what you'd pressed it for. It now decides based on the thing it's actually for. With a tilt keyframe under the playhead and no rotation key, it says Add, and adds. With a rotation keyframe there, it still offers to remove it, and a moving tilt still travels along with rotation so the two stay in step. Found by re-reading your old requests against the code.
- v11.65 — **a drawing's "draw on" animation now moves with its clip.** You can animate a drawing so it draws itself in over time, and that always worked — but the app didn't actually know those keyframes were there. So if you moved the clip along the timeline, everything else came with it and the draw-on stayed behind: the drawing would animate at the wrong moment relative to its own clip, and the keyframes never showed in the timeline row or turned up when stepping between keyframes. Now they're registered like every other animated setting, so they travel with the clip and appear where you'd expect. Deliberately limited to hand-drawn open paths: on a video, the same internal name means something completely different — how far into the footage the clip starts — and treating that as an animatable value would have broken exports and audio. Closed shapes, rectangles and videos are all explicitly checked to make sure they're left alone.
- v11.66 — **the flaky vertical-flick test was the app, not the test: a real flick sometimes just didn't glide.** A test kept failing at random and passing on the re-run, which is the worst kind of failure — it teaches you to run it again instead of read it. Ran the flick twenty times in a row and caught it: two of them dead, and not marginally so. The flick was hard, the app measured it correctly and armed the glide — and then the list sat frozen where your finger left it for the entire second and a half that followed. The cause is a detail of how browsers store scroll position: it snaps to half a pixel. The glide checked after its first frame whether the list had moved, and treated "it didn't" as "we've hit the end of the list, stop". But if that first frame arrives a fraction of a millisecond after you lift your finger — which is pure chance — the step is a third of a pixel, the snap rounds it away, and the glide cancelled itself before it started. So roughly one flick in five did nothing, on any list, with no pattern you could have described. It keeps its own position as an exact number now and rounds only when handing it to the screen, so a step too small to see still counts and the next one adds to it. Hitting a real end still stops it — that half is tested too, because "never stop" would have fixed the stall by leaving something running forever. The test that kept flickering has been replaced by one that drives the glide frame by frame with a deliberately tiny first frame, so it now fails every time the bug is present instead of one run in five.
- v11.67 — **one bad audio clip could silence your whole export, and nothing told you.** You said you'd barely done many exports so the current system might not be safe, and asked for the safety work — so I went looking in the part you haven't exercised. Found this: if a single audio file won't decode — corrupt, or a format this browser doesn't take — it didn't just lose its own sound. It took the **entire soundtrack** with it. Your music, your voiceover, every sound effect: gone, and the file exported looking perfectly normal. Measured it to be sure: two clips, one good song and one bad file, and the mix came back completely empty. The app already handled a file that decodes to nothing; a file that fails outright takes a different route out, and nothing was watching that door. Now one bad clip costs you that clip and nothing else, and it's named in the console so you know which one. **And the second half: when the soundtrack can't be built at all, the export now says so.** Four other ways of losing your audio were each made to speak up over the last few releases; this was the fifth and the widest — anything at all going wrong in the mixer landed in a log message you'd never see, and you got a silent video. A phone running out of memory on a long project ends up exactly there, which is the export you're least likely to have tried. It now shows "exporting WITHOUT SOUND" rather than quietly handing you a mute file, and the render itself still survives — a dead soundtrack must never throw away minutes of video. Both fixed with tests that fail if either protection is removed.
- v11.68 — **an export could quietly repeat frames instead of using your actual footage.** More of the export safety work. When the app builds your video it steps a clip to each frame in turn and waits for it to get there — and if it doesn't arrive within a second and a half, it gives up and uses whatever the clip was showing. That means the frame before, written into your file as though it were real. You'd have no way of knowing: the export completes, the file plays, and a moment of it is just frozen. This isn't theoretical — that wait was stretched from a quarter-second to a second and a half a while back *because* it was dropping frames on big 4K clips, which is this exact problem, answered by making the window wider rather than by noticing when it's still missed. A wider window improves the odds and can never get to zero; a slow phone or a long 4K clip is where it won't. So the misses are now counted and named — you get told how many frames repeated and the console lists which clip and which moment — instead of the file quietly claiming footage it never rendered. **And a second bug came out of testing this one:** every successful step was leaving a timer running, so a leftover from one export could fire during your next one and warn about repeated frames on a render that was perfectly fine. A warning that cries wolf stops getting read, so that's fixed too. Both directions are tested — the check fails if repeats stop being counted, and equally if a clean export starts claiming them.
- v11.69 — **the longer your export, the more crash protection you had — and then it deleted everything it saved.** Still on making export safer. A render that dies partway can now be picked up where it stopped, and to keep your phone's storage from filling up it stops saving once a render passes about nine minutes of footage. That part is fine. What it *also* did was refuse, on the way back in, every chunk it had already saved. So passing that mark didn't mean "stop saving more" — it meant "throw away the lot". A fifteen-minute export saved its first nine minutes and then, if it died, re-rendered all fifteen. And it lands on exactly the wrong ones: long renders are the most expensive to redo and the most likely to be killed, because length is what makes a phone run out of memory in the first place. Now a capped render resumes from what was saved, and the startup cleanup no longer deletes it before you get back to it. **I checked this properly rather than reasoning about it**, because a test already claimed the opposite — that resuming a capped render would leave a gap in the middle of the file. It doesn't: resuming restarts from the last saved moment, not from wherever the dead run got to. Ran a 150-frame export, capped it at frame 60, killed it at 100 and resumed: the second run rendered exactly the 90 frames that were missing, the finished file is the right length, and it's pixel-identical to a clean export at ten points across the join. The old test's claim had never been measured. The one protection that genuinely matters is untouched and still tested — a saved render from *different* export settings is still refused, because splicing that in would hand you a silently wrong video.
- v11.70 — **every time you pressed play, the first second was about a semitone sharp.** You reported audio that sounded scratchy and wrong. The main cause of that was fixed a while back — the app was nudging playback speed dozens of times a second, and each nudge makes the browser re-stretch the sound, which is the scratchy part. But that same investigation measured a second artefact and wrote it down as "noted, not fixed": playback pitching UP and sliding back at the start of every play. I re-measured it and it was still there — about 6%, roughly a semitone, over the first half-second, every single time you hit play. Here's why. The app keeps sound and picture together by measuring how far behind the audio is. Every sound device is a fixed distance behind, which isn't a problem — the app learns that distance and allows for it. The catch is it was learning it from the very first reading, taken before the sound had actually started, when the gap looks about half its real size. Measured: it learned 48 milliseconds when the truth was 87. So for the next second it believed the sound was running late and sped it up to catch up with something that was never behind. It now waits a quarter of a second — of the sound's own playing, not the clock's, so a stalled clip can't fool it — before learning anything. Result: zero speed changes on a normal play, and sync is actually TIGHTER than before (13ms out, versus a 45ms tolerance), because it's no longer chasing an error that didn't exist. Genuine drift is still corrected the moment it appears — that half is tested too, because "never correct" would have passed the first test perfectly while quietly letting your sound wander away from your video.
- v11.71 — **the Media and Audio menus were crushing the tab buttons above them — fixed, and you were right that I kept missing it.** You reported this twice and sent two screenshots: on Shape the five tabs across the top show an icon and a name; on Media the names are just gone and the row is visibly shorter. Nothing was hiding them — they were being **cut off**. The row of tabs had no instruction to hold its size, so whenever something below it wanted more room, it was the row that gave way. Media and Audio are the only two tabs that put a row of buttons AND a growing grid of your own clips underneath, so they're the only two that ever ask for more room than there is — and the names are the first thing to vanish when the row is squeezed. The row right below it already had exactly the protection it needed; the tab row never got it. One line. **Why three earlier passes at this said it looked fine:** it only happens when you actually HAVE imported clips and the sheet is short. With an empty library nothing competes for the space and the row measures perfectly — so every check that used a fresh project came back healthy. Measured with six clips in a short sheet: the row goes from 64px down to 21px and all five names disappear. Now it holds at 64px with all five, on every tab. The test stages the clips deliberately, because the clips are the thing that causes it.
- v11.71 — **you can now save a template as a file and send it to anyone.** You asked for sharing and picked files over links yourself once you knew links would need a server. A template's ⋯ menu now has **Save template file…**, which writes the same `.fmotion.json` a project already saves — so whoever you send it to can open it with the import that already exists. Nothing new to learn and no second format to go stale. It carries the layers, the media and any custom fonts the text uses, and it's named after the template rather than whatever project you happened to build it from.
- v11.72 — **the media and audio lists show three rows now, not two.** You scribbled over the empty band under your clips and said an extra row would fit. It does. Measured before changing anything: the list area is 260px tall, two rows of tiles use about 136px of it, and the ~124px left over is exactly the band you circled — three rows come to about 208px and still fit, with the spill-over still one swipe sideways rather than a scroll down. **One thing to flag, because it's your own earlier instruction:** you asked for *two* rows specifically a while back — *"I just meant two rows solid locked in then you scroll left and right"*. I've read this as a change of mind rather than a slip, because you gave a reason (the tiles got smaller) and because what you objected to then was having to scroll DOWN, which hasn't come back — the rows are still locked in and the extra clips still page sideways. Say the word and it goes back to two. Checked at every project shape, not just the one in your screenshot: the third row never pushes tiles out of view, and it isn't paid for out of the tab row above (that's the thing I fixed yesterday, and there's now a check that fails if it returns).
- v11.73 — **the undo and redo buttons are the circular arrows you asked for.** You sent a picture twice and asked for these to match it — two rings, each nearly a full circle with a solid triangular head, facing opposite ways — *"but with skinnier lines"*. They were the hooked-chevron shape before, which is a different icon entirely. Now they are that ring: a 300° sweep with a 60° gap at the top and a filled triangle at the end of the travel, undo sweeping anticlockwise and redo clockwise, drawn as an exact mirror pair. The stroke stays at the same weight as everything else in that row — that was the 'skinnier' half, and it was already true: your reference is drawn very heavy, and matching the row is thinner than the reference without making these two odd ones out. Both glyphs measure dead centre in their 24-pixel box (12.03 and 11.97 against a target of 12), which the existing centring check insists on.
- v11.74 — **Tilt Shift was ten times slower than it needed to be, and it was the slowest thing in the app by a distance.** You asked me to work on the mobile lag, so I timed **all 179 effects** at 1080x1350 — the exact size of the slow reading you sent from your phone. The median effect costs about **15ms a frame** at that size, which is already most of a frame's budget. Tilt Shift cost **776ms**. Five times the next worst, fifty times the median. One of them alone is a slideshow. The cause: it blurred by looking at seventeen neighbouring pixels for every pixel, for every colour channel, twice over — about 198 million additions per frame. A blur like that doesn't need to look seventeen times; you slide a window along and just add the pixel coming in and subtract the one going out, which is two operations instead of seventeen. **Now 74ms — 10.5 times faster — and the picture is byte-for-byte identical**, which matters more than the speed: a faster effect that draws even slightly differently would silently change every project you'd used it in. The old version is kept inside the test purely so the new one can be checked against it forever. **Worth knowing what this does and doesn't fix:** it makes the single worst effect usable, and it tells us exactly why heavy projects crawl — effects cost roughly 15ms each at full resolution, so a dozen of them cannot hit 60fps on any phone by any amount of tuning. The real answer for stacks like that is the quality ladder dropping resolution during playback, which I verified is working. This removes the one outlier that no ladder could rescue.
- v11.75 — **Spin Streaks is seven times faster.** Second in the same sweep as Tilt Shift: it cost **320ms** a frame at your project size, against a 15ms average. The reason was the same shape of waste — it was doing **22 trigonometry calls for every single pixel** (about 32 million a frame) to work out where each of the ten streak samples should come from. It didn't need any of them: every sample is just that pixel's own position spun round by a fixed amount, and spinning a known point is plain multiplication once you work out the ten angles up front — which you can do once for the whole frame instead of 1.4 million times. **Now 46ms.** Unlike Tilt Shift, this one isn't quite pixel-for-pixel identical, and I'd rather say so: the maths is exactly the same, but the two ways of computing it disagree in the last decimal place, and that occasionally tips a sample onto the neighbouring pixel. On real footage the difference is **1 or 2 shades out of 255** — invisible. On a synthetic one-pixel checkerboard it's larger, because there any change at all swings between black and white. Worth knowing: where they differ, the new one is the more accurate — the old code went out to polar coordinates and back, and that round trip is what drifts.
- v11.76 — **the biggest lag win yet, and it was the same mistake repeated sixteen times.** Sixteen effects each began by taking a full copy of the frame to read from while they overwrote it — a fresh 5.6 MB block, allocated and thrown away **every time the effect ran, every frame**. With a couple of dozen effects on a project that is about **133 MB of throwaway memory per frame**. Phones deal with that by stopping to tidy up, and a pause is exactly what "playback is a buggy mess when scrubbing is fine" feels like. They all only *read* that copy, so they can share one buffer that is created once and refilled. **Measured at your project size: Zoom Streaks 173ms → 59ms, Lens Blur 158 → 52, Tilt Shift 74 → 37, Spin Blur 102 → 70.** Three of those are effects I hadn't touched at all — the saving is the allocation, not the effect. Nothing looks different: it is the same bytes copied to the same place, just without throwing the container away each time. **Three effects were deliberately left alone** — Box Blur, Unsharp Mask and Sketch keep two or three copies at once, and handing them one shared buffer would quietly make their separate snapshots the same thing and render the wrong picture. There is now a check that fails if anyone later 'tidies' those three onto the shared buffer, because I nearly did exactly that while making this change.
- v11.77 — **the layer menu's bottom row lines up now.** You said the buttons on PC weren't showing at the right size. Measured it: **every card is exactly the same size** — all eight, 112.3px, identical. What was actually wrong is where the last row SAT. With eight buttons in a three-wide grid the last two were being centred, so they sat 60 pixels off from the columns above them — nothing lined up above or below, which reads as "these are the wrong size" even though they aren't. They now sit under the columns they belong to. Nothing was resized, so this doesn't undo your earlier ask to stop Presets and Effects being the big stretched ones. **What I could NOT reproduce is the "sometimes" part** — you said it goes wrong after playing around with it, and I drove the add menu and the layer menu back and forth at two window sizes and the cards never changed size once. So if you still see them at genuinely different sizes after this, it's a second thing and I'll need the screenshot at the moment it happens.
- v11.78 — **the add-menu buttons on PC have gradients now.** You said they'd look better with one, and they do: each card's surface is a soft ramp of its own colour, brightest at the top-left and fading out — Text blue, Captions pink, Sketching yellow, Custom shape amber, Camera violet, and so on. **No new colours were invented**: it uses the same per-button tint that was already there as a flat wash, so nothing can drift out of step with the icons. The hover state ramps up rather than jumping to a flat colour, and tiles showing your own clips keep their thumbnail — a gradient over a photo is just haze. **Scoped to PC only, as you asked.** The phone sheet uses the same buttons and I've deliberately left it alone; say the word and it gets them too. One thing worth mentioning: I first put this in a block that only applies when your device isn't set to reduce motion — which would have quietly denied the gradient to anyone using that setting, for no reason, since a gradient doesn't move. Caught it before shipping and there's now a check that fails if it ever drifts back in there.
- v11.80 — **I took yesterday's new feature back out.** v11.79 added a line telling you when an effect is switched on but does nothing to your layer — the answer to why the colouring effects looked broken. Hunting my own work the next day, I found a real fault: **the message disappeared the moment you moved a slider**, which is exactly when you'd be reading it. The detection itself was right and stayed right; the problem is that the two test renders it compares disagree for a moment after any change, so it decided the effect had started working when it hadn't. I tried one fix, measured it, and it didn't hold — so rather than leave something in that behaves like that, it's out until it works properly. **Nothing you had before this has changed.** The investigation and the tests are kept in the history, and the one question that needs answering before rebuilding it is written down.
- v11.81 — **the "this effect does nothing here" line is back, and this time it survives you using the app.** You've said three times that effects in the colouring list do nothing. They all work — the thing you were testing on couldn't show them. On your flat magenta rectangle, **Channel Remap swaps red and blue, and in that colour red and blue are both 204**; Halation blooms around bright spots a flat colour hasn't got; Long Shadow's black shadow lands on a black background. So when you open an effect that's switched on but genuinely changes nothing on that layer, a quiet amber line under its controls now says so, and names the reason where the reason is knowable. **What went wrong the first time and is fixed now:** it used to check by comparing two small preview renders, and shrinking the picture creates its own tiny differences at the layer's edge — enough to be confused with a real but subtle effect like a vignette. It now compares at your project's full size, where that noise measures exactly zero. And it only measures once you've **stopped** changing things, so dragging a slider no longer makes the message flicker away while you're reading it. If an effect is so heavy that checking would cost you a stutter, it stays silent rather than freezing the panel — I'd rather it say nothing than make the app hitch.
- v11.82 — **a stutter I added yesterday, found and removed before you hit it.** The new "this effect does nothing here" check works by drawing your project twice at full size and comparing. It runs a moment after you stop changing a setting — but nothing stopped it running *while you were playing or exporting*. So changing a slider and immediately pressing play would have dropped two full renders onto the main thread right in the middle of the frames you were watching. That's precisely the kind of hitch you've been reporting for weeks, spent on a message nobody is reading at that moment. It now waits until you've stopped, and measures then — deferred, not skipped, so the message still appears. Found by hunting my own work rather than by you hitting it.
- v11.83 — the app now ASKS to measure itself when playback is genuinely struggling: once per session, only while playing, only after the quality ladder has run out of moves and frames are still late for a couple of seconds straight, a tappable toast offers a ten-second "what's slow" sample you can copy and send. The measuring tool has existed for weeks (js/perf-probe.js) but sat four taps deep in App settings where there was no reason to find it — which is why four separate lag reports (95, 125, 202 and the original editing-lag item) have all been stuck on the same missing sentence, "needs a number from HIS phone".
- v11.84 — Turbulent Displace, the last effect still over 150ms at your project size, is 1.93x faster (148ms → 76.8ms a frame at 1080x1350). Its noise function was being evaluated four times per pixel; the first two of those depend on the column and the row separately, so they now come from two small tables built once a frame instead of ~11.7 million trig calls. Not byte-identical (the trig identities differ in the last float bits) — the maths is asserted to 1e-9, a ten-thousandth of a pixel, with the original kernel kept in the test as the reference.
- v11.85 — closed #179 (finishing a vector drawing dumping you into a full-height panel) with proof rather than another "can't reproduce": the fix had already shipped inside js/draw-tool.js, in a comment carrying Ezra's own quote and the queue number. The panel anchors under the last timeline row, and while a drawing is in progress there are no rows to measure, so it collapsed to the top of the screen; the vector branch now stops drawing BEFORE adding the layer, exactly as freehand always did. Re-verified at 380x820 on the real route (tap points → Done): layer selected, panel docked at the bottom, canvas and timeline both visible.
- v11.86 — a blank screen recording now names itself as H.265 the moment you import it, instead of fifteen seconds of nothing followed by a message that left out the fix. It only says so when the browser has stated it cannot decode HEVC AND the file's own bytes carry the hvc1/hev1 tag — both, because a confident wrong diagnosis is worse than silence. The sniff reads the head and the TAIL of the file, since an iPhone recording is written with its index at the end. And the actual fix (re-export as H.264, or open FreeMotion in Safari) is one tap away on the toast rather than in a console line you can't see on a phone.
- v11.87 — "Reset Text" (long-press the Text card) now resets to the size the app actually uses, instead of shrinking your text. The default was written down twice: the Add Text button worked it out from the project (160pt on a 1080x1920), while the layer constructor fell back to a flat 96 — and Reset copies from a pristine layer, so it was wired to the smaller of the two copies. On your portrait projects a reset made text 40% smaller; on a 2880 comp, under a third the size. One definition now, used by both. An explicitly stated size (templates, captions, AI layers) still wins, and nothing already saved is touched.
- v11.88 — opening a project that is bigger than any size the app itself offers now says so, once, with the repair one tap away: "This project is 12.2 megapixels — tap to fix the lag" opens Canvas settings and explains that leaving "Scale the layers to fit" on moves your work with it. That 12.2-megapixel project is Finding 1 of Ezra's own on-device lag report — a photograph's dimensions inherited from the first image imported into an empty comp. The cap that stops it happening (v9.27) and the repair that fixes an existing one (v9.28) both shipped months ago; nothing ever told him. It cannot fire on a 2160p comp or anything smaller, so a deliberately chosen size is never scolded.
- v11.89 — the "what's slow" report now has an AUDIO section, because three of Ezra's open reports are about sound and it said nothing about audio at all. It reports real writes to playbackRate per second, seeks, sync ticks and the median/worst sync error against the dead band — and it reads them out: a churning rate controller is named as ours (preservesPitch turns a rate write into a pitch change, heard as a scratchy warble), while a quiet one exonerates the sync loop and points at the decoder. That is exactly the fork #148 has been stuck on, waiting for his ears to settle a question the app can answer from numbers it already keeps.
- v11.90 — the export dialog now warns BEFORE you render that the file will be silent, instead of telling you during the export you have already waited for. AAC support belongs to the browser, not to your project or your settings, so it can be asked the moment the dialog opens: "This export will have no sound. This browser cannot encode AAC audio. The picture will be fine. To keep the sound, open FreeMotion in Safari and export there." It only appears when the browser really refuses AAC AND the project really has sound to lose, so a silent animation is never warned about losing audio it never had.
- v11.91 — an element saved from a SELECTION now gets a picture of those actual layers on its card, instead of a letter glyph. Saving a whole project as an element always stamped a thumbnail; the "save this selection" route never did, so every element made that way was a coloured square with a letter in it — a name and a layer count, which is fine with three elements and useless with thirty. It renders the layers being saved, not the open project, so two layers out of twenty show those two. Roughly 3-5KB each, in an index that is only written when elements change.
- v11.92 — fixed the black bar between the add menu and the timeline (#478). A raised add-menu panel floats, pinned to the grid column it measured when you grabbed the resizer — and nothing re-measured it when the WINDOW changed size. Widen the window and the column moves out from under it, leaving bare background showing between the panel and the timeline; narrow it and the panel overlaps the timeline instead. Reproduced both ways at 1440x900 (a 54px gap at 1800 wide, a 46px overlap at 1100), and it now re-pins on every resize, measured with the panel back in its grid slot.
- v11.93 — the undo/redo arrowheads are half again as big (#479). They were 3.6 units against a 14-unit ring, which at the 21px the toolbar draws them is a 3.1px nub; they are 5.4 units / 4.7px now, 39% of the ring instead of 26%. The whole glyph moved down 0.45 units to pay for it, because growing the head upward pushed the icon's ink off centre and tripped the guard from queue 410 — his own earlier complaint that these arrows sat high. Both buttons are asserted to stay the same size, mirrored, and above a floor expressed as a fraction of the ring, so the number cannot drift back down.
- v11.94 — you can finally drag a layer ON TOP of the add-layer row (#480). It was not a regression: v10.05 decided that dropping on the marker means the boundary below it, and v10.82 made the preview agree — so between two "fixes" the position above the marker became genuinely unreachable, which is what "it just teleports it back under" was. The premise both shared was wrong. The add row is itself movable, so dropping a layer on it does not need the layer order to change at all — the MARKER moves below the layer instead. The worst case was dragging the row directly beneath the marker onto it: the order is identical, so the move was a no-op by design and the row sprang back having done nothing.
- v11.95 — the "what's slow" report now measures PLAYING and SCRUBBING separately, and says which is worse. Ezra's most useful performance report is "a video will playback fine when scrubbing but actually pressing play is a buggy mess" — and this report was pooling both into a single median, the one number that cannot see that. It now prints e.g. "playing 50.0ms (28 frames) - scrubbing 16.7ms (89 frames)" and, when playing is 1.5x worse or more, states the conclusion: both draw the same frames through the same compositor, so it is not rendering cost, it is something only playback does. A bucket needs 20 frames before it is quoted, and an idle sample prints no comparison at all.
- v11.96 — the text-to-speech panel now offers the way out of its own dead end. It already explained honestly that the browser will speak your text but gives no way to record it, so the voice cannot be trimmed or exported — and the note ended "or record a voiceover yourself" without giving you any way to do that, while Record voice… already existed buried in Add > Audio. There is a "Record a voiceover instead" button under the note now. No new capability and no decision pre-empted: a recording IS an audio layer, so it trims on the timeline and lands in the export.
- v11.97 — when a "what's slow" measurement finishes, the toast is now tappable and copies the report straight to the clipboard. It used to tell you where the Copy button was: cog, canvas dialog, App settings, scroll, Copy — four or five taps on a phone, for a report the app had just asked you to produce, and five separate entries are waiting on you sending it. The old reasoning was half right (an automatic clipboard write ten seconds after the tap gets refused for want of a user gesture) — but tapping the toast IS that gesture. If the write is still refused, the toast names the four-tap route rather than failing silently.
- v11.98 — Wave, the most expensive warp effect, is 2.3x faster (24.6ms -> 10.9ms a frame at 1080x1350) and the picture is IDENTICAL — bit for bit, not merely close. Its horizontal shift depends only on the row and its vertical shift only on the column, so both sine calls, and the five parameter lookups beside them, were being recomputed 1.46 million times a frame to produce 1,080 + 1,350 distinct values. They come from two small tables built once a frame now. The test compares the two paths with === rather than a tolerance, because anything less would let a subtly different Wave through into every project that uses it.
- v11.99 — Cross Process is 9x faster (61.6ms -> 6.8ms a frame at 1080x1350) and the picture is identical, byte for byte. Its curve does a sine AND a power, and it ran three times per pixel — about 4.4 million transcendental calls a frame to produce, at most, 768 different answers, because the curve depends only on a colour value from 0 to 255. It is three 256-entry tables built once a frame now. Same idea as v11.98's Wave: the expensive maths was never really per-pixel.
- v12.00 — Lens Flare, the most expensive effect in the app, is 2x faster (71.2ms -> 36.0ms a frame at 1080x1350) with the picture identical byte for byte. It was looping all six flare rays for every pixel, wrapping each angle and taking a cosine, to find which ray that pixel lines up with — but the rays sit every 60 degrees, so the best one is simply the nearest, which is a single rounding. Six cosines and twelve wrap-tests per pixel became one cosine; and raising a number to the 32nd power became five multiplications. The original six-ray version is kept in the test as the reference and compared byte for byte.
- v12.01 — twelve more effects stopped allocating a fresh 5.6 MB copy of the frame every time they run, joining the shared buffer added in v11.76: Lens Distort (66.8ms -> 52.4), Edge (31.6 -> 23.2), Voronoi (34 -> 30), plus Pixel Sort, Dispersion, VHS Tape, Shockwave, Sharpen, Halftone, Emboss, Zoom Blur and Hex Tiles. Glitch keeps its own copies on purpose — it holds two at once, and sharing would make them secretly the same array. Also fixed the test that was supposed to be policing exactly that: its scan could only see 52 of the file's 170 effects, so it had been watching under a third of them.
- v12.02 — Contour Lines stops doing ~200x the work it needs on every effect-browser thumbnail: two of its loops were bounded by the length of the SHARED scratch buffer (which only ever grows, so after one full-size frame it stays huge) instead of the frame actually being drawn. Measured 1,451,088 wasted iterations per thumbnail, ~2.1ms each, ~418ms across a browser of 199. The picture was never wrong — the surplus writes landed past the end of a typed array, where they are silently discarded — which is why no test could see it. A new guard now scans all 29 shared-buffer effects for the same mistake, and caught the second loop I had missed while fixing the first.
- v12.03 — Dragging a layer onto the add-layer row finally puts it ABOVE the marker instead of teleporting it back underneath (queue 480). The drop was working its position out by counting rows on screen and then using that number as a position in the real layer list; a collapsed group, Edit Group or the phone's single-clip view each hide layers that still take up slots, so the two disagree and the marker lands on the wrong side. The add switch's live lean had the same fault and is fixed with it, so what you see while dragging is now where it goes.
- v12.04 — The effects browser on a PC now fits the column it actually lives in (queue 481). Docked in the inspector it is a 346px panel and was still using the wide-screen layout: featured cards drop 150px → 112px, the category tiles go from 4 columns of 71.8px squares to 3 of 100px that size themselves to their label — five names used to wrap and "Shakes / Movement" broke mid-word — the effect counts are gone, and Visual/Filters/Audio moved up into the header beside the X and the search, freeing the whole row they had to themselves. The phone sheet is untouched.
- v12.05 — Two effects had a slider that was locked in the one mode it works in (first round of the effects quality pass — the item stays open). HSL Bands on "Custom" greyed out Custom centre and Custom width and made them untouchable, so the Custom band could not actually be customised; Frame Stutter did the same to "Strobe on-time" in Strobe. The override marker was built for a tick box and then used on a drop-down, where "on" only meant "not the first option", so it fired backwards. Controls now know which option uses them, and a greyed one says "Only used when Band is Custom" rather than leaving you guessing. Found by sweeping all 345 sliders on 105 effects for range that does nothing.
- v12.06 — The undo and redo rings open up (queue 483). Their two ends were 60° apart with the arrowhead sitting on one of them, so the head and the tail nearly touched at the top; the gap is now 100°, and the arrowhead was rotated around the circle rather than nudged, so it still meets the arc at the same angle. Opening the gap moves both ends downward, so the circle's centre shifted with it — the icon now sits at 12.001 in its 24-unit box against 11.626 before, i.e. better centred than it started.
- v12.07 — Chrome and Edge no longer accuse playable iPhone videos of being unplayable (queue 486). The H.265 check asked about the bare codec name "hvc1", which Safari answers but Chromium treats as too vague — returning the same "don't know" it gives for a codec it has never heard of. Measured: "hvc1" got nothing while "hvc1.1.6.L93.B0" got "probably" on a machine with hardware HEVC decode. It now asks with the full profile and level, for both ordinary and HDR phone recordings, and still asks the short question first so Safari is unchanged.
- v12.08 — The "this project is too big" warning now reaches the project you actually come back to (queue 487).
